title: NFL predictions: Can Falcons overcome Ravens on Sunday Night Football?
description: The Falcons offense looks balanced and unstoppable, and now enters a third-straight primetime matchup: Sunday Night Football against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 5.
fullText:
The Falcons emerge from Week 4's Monday Night Football matchup with the hated Saints as glorious victors, dominating on a level I previously assumed was impossible. Atlanta's 45-24 humiliation of New Orleans on such a historic night is nothing short of astonishing, and requires a re-evaluation of what we all believed this Falcons team could be just a few weeks ago.

After an 0-2 start where the team managed just 8 points per game (32nd) under third-string quarterback Cooper Rush, the Falcons have now averaged 40 points per game (1st) under starter Michael Penix Jr. Bijan Robinson is as dominant as ever, and his complement in Brian Robinson has also impressed. The Falcons offense looks balanced and unstoppable, and now enters a third-straight primetime matchup: Sunday Night Football against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 5. The Falcons are 3.5-point home favorites per FanDuel—the first time Atlanta has been favored this season—implying a tight game, particularly if injuries impact the Ravens starting lineup.

The biggest thing to monitor heading into this game is the injury report. Baltimore seems likely to be without MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson, as he missed practice on both Wednesday and Thursday. It's not impossible for Lamar to suit up, but Atlanta will probably face veteran backup Tyler Huntley on Sunday night. This Ravens offense has been quite potent over the first four weeks of the 2026 season: 7th in scoring and 5th in total yards. But it's unlikely that type of production will continue with Huntley in the lineup, as Jackson's dynamic athleticism and playmaking ability raise the ceiling tremendously.

Baltimore's offensive line is also very banged up. The Ravens are down multiple centers are were forced to move rookie guard Vega Ioane into the middle. A trade for Cam Jurgens will provide long-term help, but Jurgens is not expected to play on Sunday. Left guard John Simpson has been limited with a groin injury, and reserve guard Andrew Vorhees (who is starting at right guard with Ioane at center) is dealing with a foot injury. Left tackle Ronnie Stanley is battling through toe and ankle injuries, but is expected to play.

This is very bad news for the Ravens, with the Falcons boasting the league's top run defense and the league's top pass rush in pressures. Atlanta's ability to dominate the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball is part of what led to their lopsided victories over the past two weeks. Baltimore is a far better opponent than either Green Bay or New Orleans, even with Tyler Huntley, but that's a tough matchup to deal with.

On the other side of the ball, top edge rusher Trey Hendrickson and corner Marlon Humphrey both missed practice to start the week. This is the best defense the Falcons have faced yet, even with those two potentially out of the lineup, both those are major losses against a red-hot offense. Atlanta is the second-best rushing attack in the NFL (including the two Cooper Rush starts) and has allowed the lowest pressure rate in the league on offense.

Those mounting injuries—along with the road trip to an Atlanta stadium that will likely be the most raucous it's been in years after two straight blowout victories—could lead to a very difficult environment for the Ravens to have success. However, this is a well-coached team that's still got talent all over the roster, and they're not just going to roll over for the Falcons.

All that being said, if Tyler Huntley plays, I'm not sure the Ravens will be able to get enough out of the passing game to keep pace with the Falcons offensively. Atlanta's defense can be vulnerable to big plays in the passing game, but I don't think Huntley is the type of quarterback who can take advantage. The Falcons will be loading up to stop Derrick Henry and crowding the short area of the field to take away quick play-action and YAC throws. This will be by far the best rushing attack Atlanta has had to defend, and we're going to learn if the team's elite run defense is capable of shutting down one of the best running backs in the NFL.

The Ravens defense will put up more of a fight than either of their past two opponents, and I'd expect Atlanta's offense to sputter a bit out of the gate. But the Falcons are simply too good on the ground to hold down for long, and the more Baltimore sells out to stop the run, the more downfield opportunities will present themselves for Michael Penix Jr. This could be a bigger test for Penix, as the Ravens will likely opt to "make Penix beat us". Working out of play-action and finding the right times to attack downfield will be critical to keep the defense honest.

An injury-marred Ravens team helmed by Tyler Huntley would've been a classic trap game for the Falcons under Raheem Morris. That's a game this team would almost always find a way to lose, despite the matchups largely falling in their favor. I know Baltimore will put up a fight regardless of who is behind center, and Atlanta should be prepared for a brawl—particularly in the first half. Atlanta starts to wear down the Ravens in the second half, and ultimately comes away with the Sunday Night Football victory, 27-20.

title: Scaling the Rocks: CarGo joins elite Colorado club
description: Colorado Rockies news and links for Friday, October 9, 2026
fullText:
We moved another step closer to the beginning of the League Championship Series as the schedule was announced on Thursday. The Milwaukee Brewers will host the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday, Oct. 11 at 6 p.m. MDT in the NLCS.

Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians have charged back and tied up their series with the Chicago White Sox to force a Game 5 on Saturday night. The Tampa Bay Rays, meanwhile, are patiently waiting after sweeping the Yankees. They wait Saturday's winner and the ALCS will begin Oct. 12 in Tampa Bay at 6 p.m. MDT.

On the local front, with football season in full swing in Denver and the Broncos grabbing most of the headlines (positive and negative), Empower Field at Mile High is completely centered on orange and blue right now. However, a Rockie will be adding a splash of purple to the stadium as Carlos González has just been inducted into the Colorado Sports Hall of Fame, which is nestled inside Mile High.

In 10 years with the Rockies, CarGo posted a 24 rWAR, connected for 227 homers and 277 doubles, while hitting .290/.349/.516 with an .865 OPS. The outfielder was named to three National League All-Star rosters, earned three Gold Gloves and two Silver Sluggers and won the NL batting title in 2010 when he hit .336.

Read about his selection and more news from around MLB below.

Rockies' Car-Go, Broncos' Nalen among newly elected Colorado Sports Hall of Famers | 9News.com

CarGo, a fan favorite known as the Rockie with the sweetest swing, is one of six athletes to join the elite group, which will be inducted officially on April 15, 2027, at a banquet at the Hilton Denver City Center.

Other Rockies in the Colorado Sports Hall of Fame include Dante Bichette, Vinny Castilla, Andrés Galaraga, Todd Helton, and Larry Walker, along with Colorado's first manager Don Baylor, first general manager Bob Gebhard, and former team president Keli McGregor.

Rockies plan for 2027 'as if we're not going to have' Kris Bryant | DenverSports.com (The Fan 104.3)

Not breaking news, as this was covered in the Rockies press conference from Tuesday, but the Kris Bryant situation is always worth remembering. At least Colorado president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta talked about it, which seemed vital after Bryant didn't play and was never around in 2026.

Each team's all-time postseason home run leader | MLB.com

You have to narrow it to the years the Rockies went to the playoffs: 1995, 2005, 2007, 2017, and 2018. So it has to be either from the Rocktober era or lone back-to-back postseason berths era.

It turns out it's the first option: it's Matt Holliday with five playoff bombs. What's even more wild is that Holliday only had one season — 2007 — with the Rockies in the postseason.

Predicting the Outcome for Each MLB Team's Top 2026-27 Free Agent | Bleacher Report

Joel Reuter picked Rockies veteran pitcher Kyle Freeland. Freeland, 33, just pitched his 10 season in Colorado. With his contract ended, Reuter predicts that the Rockies bring him back and hope that he can have a bounce-back season.

MLB proposes 154-game schedule, new playoff features | MLB.com

On Thursday, the latest proposal from MLB went to the MLB Players Association and included some changes that would begin in 2029. One is a season with eight fewer games and a weekly off-day for each team. Another is a change to the postseason for the Division Series that would increase each league's contests from five-game series to seven games. In addition, the top seeds from the Wild Card round and Division Series round would get to pick their opponents, allowing for the bracket to be altered each round.

The Rays are known for doing more with less. Here are 5 case studies | The Athletic ($)

Outside of the White Sox, the Rockies can also always look to the Tampa Bay Rays for a model of how to scout, draft, develop and build a low-cost roster in a small market. The Rays do it year in and year out, but no other team seems able to replicate their success. This article look at five players that were castoffs from other teams before finding their way in Tampa Bay.

'Maniac' Baker is on the most dominant run a Rays closer has ever had

There are many reasons the Rays are good. Bryan Baker, the 31-year-old All-Star closer is a big one. He recorded saves in all three games against the Yankees. He joined elite company in that feat, joining former Rockies closer Manny Corpas (2007), as well as Mark Wohlers (1996) and Dennis Eckersley (1988 and '96), as the only pitcher to get three saves in his team's first three postseason games. Baker is the only one to do it without giving up a hit.

It's Never Going to Happen With Aaron Boone | The Ringer

New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone is on the hot seat. Maybe.

After another early exit from the postseason, the second in a row in the ALDS, New York has to be reassessing its personnel. The Yankees haven't won a World Series since 2009.

title: DeMeco Ryans is taking back play-calling duties. Can the change provide a spark for Texans' defense?
description: Houston Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans made the decision to take over play-calling. But how much will it truly help?
fullText:
The first sign that the Houston Texans were having issues on defense came on the third play of the second half of their 34-30 loss to the Dallas Cowboys last Sunday.

Wide receiver CeeDee Lamb ran a post route against the Texans' zone defense, heading toward the middle of the field. Cornerback Derek Stingley Jr., who initially lined up in front of Lamb, passed off his assignment shortly after Lamb planted his foot and cut toward the left corner.

But whoever was responsible for picking up Lamb as he crossed into the left quadrant of the field apparently never heard the call.

When Lamb caught the pass from quarterback Dak Prescott, no one was within 10 yards of him, allowing him to gain an additional 11 yards on a 30-yard catch deep inside Texans territory.

The Texans' defense allowed four explosive pass plays - passes of 20 yards or more - in the second half alone, not including the 12-yard touchdown pass to Lamb that put the Cowboys ahead for good.

Missed opportunities and communication issues have been recurring themes for Houston's defense, which ranked No. 1 in the NFL in total yards allowed per game last year. The Texans were considered Super Bowl contenders this offseason largely because of the defense's reputation as a top-ranked unit that returned all but one of its starters.

But this year, one thing everyone can agree on is that the communication has been off.

Through four games this season, the Texans have given up 17 pass plays of 20 yards or more, second most in the NFL behind the Detroit Lions, who have allowed 20.

"If there's a lack in communication, I look at myself first," coach DeMeco Ryans said Wednesday. "It starts with me and making sure I'm a better communicator. Just to help spark things more, I'm going to take over the play calling for the defense.

"I'm going to make sure that communication is right."

Ryans' decision to take over play-calling duties came as little surprise.

He called the plays during his first two seasons as the Texans' head coach and the first three games of the 2025 season. He delegated that responsibility to defensive coordinator Matt Burke after an 0-3 start last season so he could focus on helping the offense.

The move worked. The offense found some consistency, and the defense remained dominant.

Houston went on to win 12 of its next 14 games and made the playoffs for the third consecutive season.

Ryans hopes this change, though in reverse, will provide a similar spark for his defense, which is currently ranked 20th in yards allowed per game (343.8) and 26th in points allowed per game (27.3).

"Me taking over play calling duties is just to spark some change," Ryans said. He added that it was no slight to Burke, whom he said did an "outstanding job."

"Make sure we streamline communications. Make sure we're all flying around on the same page. Clear mind, fast feet, let's go fly around, play some football."

The play calling in Sunday's game likely won't look much different from when Burke was calling the plays.

Though Burke had the autonomy to make any call he thought would work, Ryans, who was also on the headset, had the power to veto a play if he preferred, two team sources said.

Ryans also collaborated with Burke on the defensive game plan, they added.

In other words, Ryans had his hands on every part of the defensive plan, while Burke made the in-the-moment judgment calls.

"A little disappointed," Burke said Thursday when asked about the decision. "Really not even about me. I think we're all disappointed in where we're at and how we performed and being 0-4 at this point.

"So DeMeco and I have a really honest relationship, and he just said, 'I think we need to spark a change.' And I said, 'OK, what do you need from me?' And he said, 'I just need to keep game planning and working the plan with me for the week,' the same as we've always done."

Burke wasn't sure whether the change was permanent or temporary. He said that when they had the conversation earlier this week, they didn't discuss the time frame.

He said his weekly duties will likely remain the same for the time being, but on game day he'll instead be the voice in Ryans' headset, telling him what to be aware of as the head coach prepares to make play calls.

It was the same role Ryans had when Burke was calling the plays.

The communication between players and coaches could see the biggest difference.

Ryans will deliver whatever message he sees fit directly to the defense, rather than having Burke deliver it.

"I think it will let us go out there and play fast, with no confusion," safety Calen Bullock said. "Everybody is in position that they are comfortable in, and go out there and make plays."

Making plays has been one of the biggest things missing from this defense this season.

While the Texans' defense has recovered two fumbles, its secondary has just one interception. In 2025, the Texans were among the best at creating takeaways, especially through the air.

Bullock, cornerbacks Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter, and nickelback Jalen Pitre each finished the regular season with four interceptions.

But none of those players has recorded an interception this year.

Stingley and Bullock both said they weren't worried about it, though.

"We know we can't go out there chasing plays," Stingley told the Chronicle. "You've just got to keep playing. The ball will start coming your way, and just capitalize on it.

"I think we were in the same spot last year. In the first couple of games nobody could really get one. But once somebody got one, then we started rolling."

Ryans believes the interceptions are coming for the secondary.

"You look at the game this past week, we attacked the throwing arm of the quarterback three times, and three times the ball goes up and they come down with the completion," Ryans said. "I've never seen that happen. Sometimes the ball has to kind of fall your way, and it's coming."

Sunday's game against the Titans might be one of the Texans' best opportunities to get things started.

Titans quarterback Cam Ward, who is in his second season, has struggled this season. He has thrown an interception in each of his last two games.

The Texans are 2-0 all time against Ward, including their Week 4 win last year that sparked their run after an 0-3 start.

The Texans had one takeaway in that 26-0 win - an interception by Stingley, who returned it 20 yards.

As Ryans takes back the reins, he's hoping to see more of that.

"We're getting back to our style, our brand of football," Ryans said. "If we keep attacking the ball, it'll keep coming."

title: Jaiden Lo Re and DJ Layton made some noise in their first professional season
description: The two former mid round picks flashed upper echelon skills that may put them on the path to Baltimore
fullText:
The Orioles haven't made a lot of noise outside the early rounds of the draft under Mike Elias. Of the Elias draftees currently on the 40-man roster, only Coby Mayo was drafted outside the top 100 picks of a draft (Mayo was pick 103 in the 4th round in 2020). However, with fast-rising prospects Jaiden Lo Re and DJ Layton, Elias may have found some mid-round picks that could turn into future major leaguers.

Lo Re was one of the true breakout players throughout the organization. The high school SS out of Scottsdale, AZ wasn't one of MLB.com's top 200 prospects for the 2025 draft, but caught the eye of Elias and his scouting department. Baltimore took the now 19-year-old with the 154th pick in the 2025 draft and signed him for an above-slot-value $562,500 to lure him away from a BYU commitment.

Despite being drafted in July of 2025, the 5'11", switch-hitting infielder didn't make his minor league debut until the start of the 2026 season. The Orioles chose to start him off in rookie ball, as he made his pro debut in early May. Lo Re only lasted 20 games in the Florida Complex League, however, thanks to his red-hot start to the year. In 65 ABs at rookie ball, Lo Re slashed .354/.421/.462 while walking 9 times against 6 Ks and adding 7 stolen bases.

That impressive showing earned Lo Re a step up to Low-A Delmarva at the beginning of June. In his first month with the Shorebirds, the infielder continued to be an on-base machine. In his first 20 games with Delmarva, Lo Re hit .333 with a .471 OBP, as he collected 23 hits and walked 18 times against just 8 strikeouts. July in Salisbury saw the 19-year-old cool off just a little, as he only slashed .299/.377/.433, but did start a 12-game hitting streak.

He started to show a little more pop in August, launching 6 doubles and a triple while hitting .343 and posting a .926 OPS. That final hot stretch for the Shorebirds earned Lo Re a late-season promotion to High-A Frederick. In his first seven games with the Keys, the teenager definitely showed signs of going through an adjustment. In his first 19 ABs for Frederick, Lo Re hit only .158 with a .638 OPS. However, he turned it around to end the year, slashing .387/.406/.484 across his last 7 games of the year to truly establish himself at High-A.

The former 5th-round pick also went from high school infielder to professional utility man in his first season as a professional. Split across the three levels he played at in 2026, Lo Re logged 100+ innings at 2B, SS, 3B and CF. One professional season in A-ball is far from enough to know if he'll make it to Baltimore one day. But early returns on the Arizona native paint a picture of a Blaze Alexander-like player.

Charting a similar path in 2026 was fellow utility man DJ Layton. The 20-year-old came to the Orioles' organization as a 6th-round pick (189th overall) in the 2024 draft. He was another high school SS whom the O's paid over slot value for, giving out a $715,800 bonus to get Layton to forgo his Southern Miss commitment. The 2025 season saw little to write home about for Layton, who hit .183 with a .597 OPS in 40 games in rookie ball.

Despite that inauspicious start to his professional career, the Orioles promoted Layton to Delmarva to begin the 2026 season. Early on, that move paid off for Layton and the Shorebirds. Through his first 22 games with Delmarva, Layton hit .284 with a .896 OPS while walking 20 times and stealing 8 bags.

The 20-year-old's performance dipped in May, with his average dropping to .250 and OPS dipping to .765. Those struggles continued into June, with his average dipping further down to .214, his power nearly non-existent with a .343 slugging percentage and a still declining OPS at .732.

Layton began to turn it around as the calendar turned to July, eventually earning a promotion to Frederick at the beginning of August. Over his last 30 games with the Shorebirds, his average ticked up to .242 while posting an elite .390 on-base percentage. When the switch-hitting utility man was promoted to Frederick on August 11th, he signed off on a Low-A career that saw him slash .247/.396/.389 with 73 walks and 32 stolen bases.

The North Carolina native opened up his High-A account with a 3-for-4 night that included his first Keys home run. He'd settle back to being much the same hitter he was at Low-A after that. Over 25 games with Frederick, Layton slashed .238/.390/.393 while walking 21 times and stealing 13 bases.

At this point, Layton is more projection than production. He's a high-level athlete with 65-grade speed and a 60-grade arm. Eventually, that may turn into more over-the-fence production, but that's yet to show up. In 117 games across the two levels of A-ball, he only hit 8 homers while collecting 25 doubles.

What he does extremely well already is get on base and create havoc on the base paths. He walked 92 times in 489 PAs, an 18.8% walk rate that would've led the majors by almost two whole percentage points. His 45 stolen bases were also one more than 80-grade speedster Enrique Bradfield Jr. His athleticism should also allow him to stick at a premium position long term, with Layton playing 500+ innings at SS in 2026 while also seeing significant time in CF and at 2B.

title: Detroit Tigers News: MLB proposes shortened regular season, Kevin McGonigle wins another award
description: Baseball America names Kevin McGonigle the overall Rookie of the Year.
fullText:
The preparation continues for this impending misery of an offseason. MLB and the players union have already been lobbing proposals at each other for months, and this will no doubt continue as either side tries to position itself and lobby the fanbase in advance of the next collective bargaining agreement negotiations this winter. MLB came back with a new round of ideas on Thursday, and the reception was tepid.

Kevin McGonigle's march to the AL Rookie of the Year award continued as Baseball America named the Tigers' infielder their 2026 Rookie of the Year. Their prospect tools review of the 2026 draft also had some Tigers mentioned.

Both league championship series are taking shape, and so we'll also link you to some playoff previews as the Dodgers and Brewers prepare for an epic showdown, while the Rays await the winner of the White Sox-Guardians series. The Guardians looked cooked early in Game 4 until Jose Ramirez finally provided some of his old spark, and his teammates took it to the White Sox's bullpen to force a decisive Game 5.

Kevin McGonigle is Baseball America's overall Rookie of the Year for 2026. The article points to the fact that McGonigle is so good at everything, rather than having one obvious strength, as the reason he's already thriving at the major league level.

They also link of list of players 21 and under this season who accumulated at least 1 WAR per Baseball Reference. That is a record number of players that age putting up that kind of value.

Cody Stavenhagen of the Athletic reports that the Tigers have fired Head Athletic Trainer Ryan Eubanks, as well as Assistant Athletic Trainer Chris MacDonald. The incredible number of soft tissue, non-contact injuries suffered by the Tigers this season no doubt played a role. The Tigers have already parted ways with long-time assistant pitching coach Juan Nieves, as well as first base coach Anthony Sanders. After the way this season went there are probably more changes coming. I'll not again that the Tigers still don't have a director of pitching in the minor leagues almost a year after Gabe Ribas left to join the Colorado Rockies coaching staff.

Rogelio Castillo, writing for Tigers Roundtable, considers the case of Colt Keith, who continues to be a modestly above average run producer, but still doesn't have a defensive home.

Baseball America did its annual look at best tools from each team's new draft class. As you'd expect, first rounder Cameron Flukey gets the highest marks for his fastball, which is among the best in the whole draft class, as well as his pair of breaking balls. They also mention second rounder Tyson LeBlanc's breakout with the bat this season, calling his the best hit tool in the Tigers' draft class, while fourth rounder Dominic Pellegrin gets high marks for his speed and defensive ability. The minor leagues and the NPB already both have Monday off for the whole league outside of special exceptions. MLB also floated the idea that top seeds in the postseason should get to pick their opponent, as well as expanding the divisional round to best-of-seven formats. Simply put, they want more lucrative postseason baseball to broadcast, and cutting back regular season games allows them to trim some player payroll as well.

MLB also sent a memo to teams on lockout procedures that was quickly leaked, and while it's all standard, it is also amusingly petty stuff, for legal reasons.

Ben Whitelaw looks at the Tampa Bay Rays increased offspeed pitch usage as the club's next evolution. The Tigers are working in this direction as well, ranking 10th in offspeed pitch usage this season, while the Rays were first.

title: Hubert Hurkacz reacts after beating Novak Djokovic for the first time in Shanghai, ‘It’s a special night’
description: Hubert Hurkacz defeated Novak Djokovic, 6-4, 6-3, in the second round of the Shanghai Masters. The Pole produced a serving masterclass to snap Djokovic’s winning...
fullText:
Hubert Hurkacz defeated Novak Djokovic, 6-4, 6-3, in the second round of the Shanghai Masters.

The Pole produced a serving masterclass to snap Djokovic's winning streak in China. Djokovic won the China Open earlier in the week and was looking to pick up another title in Shanghai, but it wasn't to be.

Having lost their first eight encounters, Hurkacz finally defeated Djokovic, securing his place in the third round of the Shanghai Masters. Always humble in victory or defeat, Hurkacz shared some kind words about the 24-time Grand Slam champion after the match.

"It's a special night. I've been playing Novak [Djokovic] for like seven years, and it's always been unsuccessful, but he presents such a great challenge, such a great champion. For so many years, he's been on the tour on the top; he just won Beijing, so it's a very difficult task to play against him," said Hurkacz.

2023 Dubai Tennis Championships – QF

Novak Djokovic and Hubert Hurkacz's head-to-head record

"But it's also a pleasure to share a court with him, to play such a legend of the sport; it's a lot of fun, and then you challenge also yourself, you find where your level is."

"Definitely, it was very important at the start to stay with Novak, because if he gets ahead, he presents such a great level, it's not easy to come back," he said when asked to pinpoint the key moments of the match.

"Then, of course, towards the end, I was feeling some nerves, it's not the first time leading by a break in the decider against Novak, so I was definitely trying to stay focused, focus on my things and what I needed to do, and then I was pleased with the performance at the end."

Hurkacz was simply the better player on the day and deserved the win. His serve guided him to victory as it so often does, but it would be unfair not to praise other areas of his game. The 2023 Shanghai Masters champion played excellent tennis throughout and will be one to watch at the year's penultimate Masters 1000 event.

Second serve points won % – 53%

Average second serve speed – 164 km/h

The 29-year-old will return to play Zhou Yi or Lorenzo Musetti in the third round this weekend. If he wins that match, Hurkacz will meet Frances Tiafoe or Alejandro Davidovich Fokina in the last 16.

Djokovic was as positive as we've seen him for months after winning the China Open on Tuesday. During his post-match press conference, the Serb seemed upbeat about his chances going forward.

"Of course, I'm very proud of the achievement here. It came at the best possible time as a confidence booster, as proof that I can still play at the highest level. Winning against three top-10 players in a matter of three days back-to-back is a great achievement. I'm obviously filled with joy," he said.

Unfortunately, his Shanghai Masters performance left a lot to be desired and may have reset those expectations. When at his best, Djokovic remains one of the best in the world, but at 39, he's simply unable to produce that level for as long and as often as some of his younger rivals.

Losing to Hurkacz in Shanghai also hurt Djokovic's chances of qualifying for the ATP Finals. He remains in the final qualification spot, but could be overtaken by several players, including Alex de Minaur and Rafael Jodar, by the end of the tournament.

"It's always nice to have a bit of a break and use the cup games to try new things. I think we all are ready to get back into league action now and pick up from where we left off. It'll be nice to be back at home as well.

title: How Cadillac’s Formula 1 Team Is Struggling to Find Stability and Success
description: The VP of Global Motorsport at General Motors and the team’s top exec talk challenges, potential, and necessary next steps.
fullText:
Eric Warren worked in defense and at NASA prior to his current role as vice president for Global Motorsport Competition at General Motors. Top tier motor racing isn't rocket science; in many ways it's more difficult than that. "I hesitate to say we should have won," he says of Cadillac's performance earlier this year in the 24 Hours of Le Mans (with Hertz Team Jota), "but we certainly could have won, and that's a big step forward."

The truth is, GM has serious form here, more than it gets credit for, with lots more to come. Ford's motorsport-crazy C.E.O. Jim Farley is a passionate, high-profile advocate for the Blue Oval's racing exploits, but GM comfortably eclipses Ford in terms of multidiscipline commitment. WEC, IMSA, NASCAR, IndyCar, the NHRA, off-road truck racing, Australian supercars—GM is highly active in all of it.

First Drive: Bugatti's Bolide Hypercar Is a Meteoric Machine on Miami's F1 Circuit

Tyrese Gibson and Cody Walker on Bringing the 'Fast & Furious' Franchise to Life With Their FuelFest Tour

Lewis Hamilton Bought His Dream Car, the Iconic Ferrari F40

But it's Cadillac's presence in Formula 1 that's indicative of the mothership's ambitions for its increasingly impressive luxury brand. From zero to debuting at the Australian GP earlier this year was no mean feat, and it earned the hat-tip respect of rivals. But for all that F1 is as a globally effective shop window with unparalleled reach among key new demographics, simply showing up is categorically not enough. Cadillac has endured some persistent reliability issues and needs to surmount them.

"We want to compete for wins. We wouldn't be in it if we didn't plan on competing for wins—in every category we're racing in worldwide, not just F1," Warren says firmly. "I've been around some defense industry stuff, NASA is my background, and I've seen a lot of amazing things. But these new F1 engines are incredible. These are tools that are working hard. You're also constantly analyzing data. There's no more data-rich environment than this."

As the F1 season heads onto the home straight, and with both the Austin and Vegas Grands Prix races in prospect, it's a useful time to recap how the U.S. newcomer has been doing. GM's big F1 play, of course, grew out of Andretti Motorsport's bid to become the 11th team in the elite race series. As ever in this intensely political world, various forces had to align, and big names placated, before things could progress. Existing stakeholders had to be mollified so that F1's prize fund could grow to accommodate a new team rather than be diluted. (I recall Christian Horner, former principal for the Red Bull F1 Team, being especially vocal on this matter.)

Dan Towriss, C.E.O. of TWG Motorsports (and now of the Cadillac Formula 1 Team as well), assumed control of the bid, and made the approach. Towriss has the energy and vibe of one of the main characters in Showtime's Billions saga. GM's vice president of Performance and Motorsports, Jim Campbell, remembers meeting him and his wife in a lift on the way to an IndyCar function a few years ago. Had GM thought about F1? "It really was an elevator pitch," Campbell says. Internally, the conversations began in 2022.

"We saw the potential and you could argue we got in on it a little bit late," Warren attests. "But we're still pretty early on the growth cycle. It was a matter of opportunity. It was important that we didn't just sponsor, we want to be a critical part of it, to collaborate fully. We get in and race in all the series we do, although we support teams differently in each. If we come in, we're coming in as partners. Strategy platforms, tools, setups, simulators, aero, CFD . . . everything that it takes to design and build a car, we do."

The opportunity to partner with TWG was key, but so too was the introduction of the cost cap in F1 (initiated in 2021, set at $215 million for 2026). Technical transfer for Cadillac and throughout the wider group is part of the mission, but anyone who has attended an F1 race recently will know that the brand-building possibilities are phenomenal—think Coachella with a motor race attached. The so-called "fan zones" are becoming bigger and more ambitious at every race. "We want to build the Cadillac brand, for the fans. The demographic is changing and getting younger. A lot of things are lining up," Campbell says.

As is the direction of travel on the power-train front. F1's nominal 50-50 internal combustion/electric hybrid format has proven controversial at best and is actively disliked by many of the drivers. The farcical situation that unfolded at last weekend's Bahrain GP–held in Sepang, in Malaysia–has only deepened the malaise: a software bug left Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen, and others stranded on the track prior to a system reboot and restart. It was not a good look.

The auto manufacturers who are the commercial mainstays of Formula 1 demand an emphasis on electrification and sustainability. But the requirements for energy management and power-starved engines have compromised pure racing—particularly in terms of overtaking and cornering speeds—throughout the 2026 season. Although, as ever, it depends on who you ask.

Cadillac is currently constructing a power-train manufacturing facility in Concord, N.C, bolstering bases in Silverstone and Indiana, the aim being for the team to have its own engine good-to-go for the 2029 season. (It's currently using Ferrari's power unit.) The proposed return to a V-8 is presumably good news for the all-American team, right?

"We need to work in both directions, the hybrid V-6, the current platform, but also keep an eye on the V-8," says Warren cautiously. "Our statement on this is that we want to support the series. Certainly, we have a lot of products with V-8s in the Americas. It's in the Cadillac hypercar. We do lots of engines, we've raced in a lot of series . . . We like the sound of a [V-8], a lot of the elements, get some cost out of it . . . there's a lot of positives, but I think it's about trying to support the series. We want something that's exciting for the fans and the competitors, and for the series."

Is it imperative that Cadillac runs an American driver? Warren plays it down. Finding the home-grown equivalent of Mercedes-AMG's break-out superstar Kimi Antonelli is desirable but not essential. "We want to be authentically American, certainly regarding ownership and everything. But we want to race competitively. There's a pathway to get to that, but just putting an American in there when the car's not ready or the team's not ready, just to say it's American, no. We want to continue progressing and we knew it was going to be hard," Warren continues. "It's difficult for me to say that we're happy, because every week you want to see progression. We're proud of what it's taken to get here. But there's a difference being proud and being happy . . . that's the long-term goal. We won't be happy until we compete for wins."

It also seems that patience in getting to that point is decidedly finite. Robb Report spoke to Graeme Lowdon, Cadillac's team principal, during the Hungarian GP earlier this year. A well-liked figure in the paddock, Lowdon was instrumental in realizing Cadillac's F1 dream from a blank sheet of paper. Personnel, infrastructure, design, engineering, coffee machines—the lot.

"We're not just here to make up the numbers. We have a bold ambition to build a substantial and successful team, but it does take some time," Lowden explained when we spoke. "I was talking to another team principal, discussing a particularly successful stage at one team. 'Yeah, you know the reason for that success was the six years of failure beforehand,' he reminded me. People forget just how long it takes to get there. But this is a sport where it's maximum attack all the time on every front. The common denominator in sustained success is stability."

Note the past tense in describing Lowdon's role. When I mentioned to Lowdon that figures like Dan Towriss aren't generally known for being patient, he forced a smile. It's likely to have been the last interview he did as Cadillac's team principal. Despite his insistence on stability, Towriss evidently disagreed. Lowdon was fired shortly after we spoke, and had no inkling it was coming.

"It wasn't a mutual decision," Towriss explained in a media call shortly after. "The process started a few months ago: really thinking about what the next phase for Cadillac Formula 1, what's the right timing, how would that look, and then the capabilities of the various folks out there."

Cadillac F1's new team principal is ex-Alpine F1 executive director Marcin Budkowski. With the team up and running, improving on-track competitiveness is now critical. As we head into this weekend's Singapore GP, the team has come tantalizingly close but has yet to score any championship points. One of its drivers, Valtteri Bottas, elected to ride a bicycle from Kuala Lumpur to Singapore rather than fly. It's a distance of around 220 miles, which should give him time to think.

"There's no easy way to make this transition within Formula 1 . . . It does compress the decision-making, the timeline, and how these things come together," Towriss admits. "It makes it feel more abrupt than it would otherwise be. But it's the nature of Formula 1 and it's the way it had to happen." Formula 1 is famously known as the "piranha club." Results are all that matter. And while Cadillac has arrived, it must now prove as hungry and aggressive as the others.

title: How can Ohio State football beat Maryland? 3 keys for Buckeyes' homecoming game
description: Ohio State hosts Maryland in its lone home game in October. Here are the factors that could help it prevail against the Terrapins.
fullText:
Here are three keys for No. 6 Ohio State against Maryland on Oct. 10:

Maryland operates at one of the fastest tempos in the country, averaging 23.6 seconds per play, a pace that ranks 12th in the Football Bowl Subdivision, according to TeamRankings.com. The up tempo has not led to a surge in scoring. Its 30.4 points per game are only in the middle of the pack. But the Buckeyes have not seen an offense that plays as quickly as the Terrapins. Their previous fastest opponent this season was Texas, which averages two more seconds between snaps. It could require an adjustment from a defense that has used heavy personnel rotations as it incorporates new pieces. The Buckeyes will need to disrupt the Terrapins' rhythm and get them off schedule.

The Buckeyes allowed four sacks last week at Iowa, nearly as many as the five they had surrendered in their first four games. Heavy blitzing caused the issues, as all four times quarterback Julian Sayin hit the turf followed instances of the Hawkeyes bringing extra pressure, per Pro Football Focus. The pass protection and blitz pickup will need to be better against the Terrapins, who are third in the Big Ten with 14 sacks. Linebacker DD Holmes and defensive tackle Derrick LeBlanc lead Maryland's pass rush with 2.5 sacks apiece, and defensive end Eyan Thomas also has two sacks.

Most teams have experienced slow starts against Maryland, which has allowed seven or fewer points in the first quarter in 21 consecutive games, the sixth-longest active streak in the Football Bowl Subdivision. Both Nebraska and UCLA turned the ball over against the Terrapins in the opening frame in the previous two weeks. While the Bruins would total 54 points in a lopsided rout, it was not until their fourth drive that they reached the end zone. The gap between these sides is wide enough that the Buckeyes should also be able to overcome a sluggish start, but it would less than ideal the week before they visit Indiana for a rematch of last year's Big Ten title game.

Ohio State passing defense vs. Maryland passing offense

The Terrapins will test the Buckeyes' secondary by virtue of their high-volume passing game. Only Hawaii and Cal have thrown the ball more through five weeks. Malik Washington is the triggerman, leaning on Chris Durr Jr., a Wyoming transfer who has the second-most receptions among Big Ten wide receivers after Jeremiah Smith. Durr has caught 42 passes for 461 yards and four touchdowns. But Maryland's aerial attack can be a double-edged sword. Washington has thrown more interceptions (six) than touchdowns (one) in two conference games, and three of the picks were returned for touchdowns. The competitiveness of this matchup is likely to hinge on whether Maryland can find more success through the air. If not, the Buckeyes are likely to capitalize on mistakes.

2: Wins by Maryland in its last 20 Big Ten games, a stretch that began with the start of conference play in 2024.

title: Dolphins acquire former first-round pick in mock trade
description: The Miami Dolphins could really use more help at wideout, so they may be willing to part with a 2027 draft pick to bring in a former first rounder.
fullText:
After moving on from Mike McDaniel and Chris Grier, the Miami Dolphins, under new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley, turned over a big portion of their roster over the offseason.

With that came big changes in the wide receiver room. Instead of Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle being the top guys, the Dolphins are rolling with Malik Washington and the rookie trio of Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr. as the best options for new quarterback Malik Willis.

So far, the results haven't been great, as the Dolphins are 0-4, and without Douglas against the Minnesota Vikings, Willis threw for less than 100 yards. Adding more help at the position could be beneficial for Miami's offense going forward.

Interestingly, Bleacher Report's Alex Kay recently suggested that the Dolphins trade a 2027 third-round pick to the Jacksonville Jaguars for wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr.

Thomas, 24, played at LSU from 2021-23, earning All-SEC honors and leading the NCAA in receiving touchdowns in 2023. Jacksonville took the wideout in the first round of the 2024 NFL Draft, and he had a strong rookie season, catching 87 passes for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns on his way to a Pro Bowl.

Last year, Thomas' production dipped, as he hauled in 48 passes for 707 yards and just two touchdowns, and now through four games this year, he's on pace for just 38 receptions, 446 yards and four scores.

The 6-foot-2 receiver proved he could find success in the NFL as a rookie, but with his perfromance since then, he might need a change of scenery, and Miami should be interested in adding him to the room for Willis, and/or whoever is under center in 2027.

title: Hoeneß reacts to Jeltsch missing out on Germany debut

fullText:
20-year-old Finn Jeltsch was included in Germany's squad for the recent UEFA Nations League games against Serbia and Greece, but will have to wait a little longer for his senior international debut, having remained an unused substitute in both matches.

For VfB Stuttgart coach Sebastian Hoeneß, however, there is no doubt that the young centre-back will eventually represent his country at senior level.

"Of course, Finn would have liked to make his debut. But it's only a matter of time before that happens. He told us that he had an incredible amount of fun, that there was great energy within the team and that he enjoyed being part of it," Hoeneß told reporters.

Having established himself as a regular starter in Stuttgart's defence, Jeltsch has attracted interest from several European top clubs.

"Finn has a bright future ahead of him. He is very eager to learn. If he maintains that attitude, he will only get better, even though he is already performing at a very good level," Hoeneß predicted.

title: Bo Nix insists he’s healthy, but the QB isn’t running as often as last season
description: Broncos quarterback Bo Nix insists he's healthy and feels great, but the third-year QB isn't running as often as he used to.
fullText:
Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix reiterated this week that he's healthy following a report that he's had some swelling and stiffness in his ankle after activity and flights this season.

"I feel great. I'm healthy," Nix said after Wednesday's practice. "I feel as good as I've felt in a long time, and honestly my GPS numbers during games are telling me that. So I'm really excited about that."

That's Nix's message, but his actions might tell a different story. The quarterback has rushed for 25 yards through the first four games of the 2026 season. Last year, Nix averaged 20.9 rushing yards per game, and he totaled 78 yards on the ground through the first weeks of the 2025 season.

When asked about not running as often as he did last season, Nix suggested that checking the ball down to running back RJ Harvey is a better option than using his own legs.

"I'll ask you all, do you all want me with the ball or RJ with the ball?" Nix asked reporters. "RJ. Don't hesitate. Don't think twice about it. You all want RJ with the football."

“Y’all want RJ with the football.”

Bo Nix explains his checkdown decisions and why he hasn’t been scrambling as much. #broncoscountry pic.twitter.com/HKeTKMvxc4

Nix insisted that he'll run when he believes it's the right decision. So far, he's viewed a checkdown to Harvey as the better choice more often than not this fall.

"I'm going to be extremely confident when my time comes to pull it down and run, but at the same time, you keep seeing RJ and those guys doing what they're doing with the ball with their hands," Nix said. "It's like, 'Get it to the outlet, and let's move the ball forward.'"

Up next for Nix and Co. is a road showdown with the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 5. Denver's offense has been sluggish so far this season, and Nix has appeared reluctant to use his legs as often as he did from 2024-2025. Perhaps that will change on Sunday. If not, expect another big receiving game from Harvey out of the backfield.

title: Anatomy of a scandal: The story of sandpapergate and how Australia got caught
description: LONG READ: Australia arrived in South Africa amid simmering hostility and left in disgrace, writes Lawrence Ostlere. But, as they prepare to return to Cape Town eight years on, there remain uncomfortable questions about who knew what
fullText:
What made South Africa so suspicious? Well, there was a strange request by the Australian camp before the series began to turn down the volume on the stump mics. The inference was that the tourists were planning a confrontational approach in the middle, but the request was a "surefire way of making sure it stays turned up", one commentator later told The Australian. It put the entire broadcast booth on alert.

Then there was the devastating swing Australia's bowlers generated during the first Test in Durban, when Mitchell Starc had the ball on a string. There was no evidence Australia had tampered, but something didn't feel right to South Africa captain Faf du Plessis, and for the rest of the series he kept a pair of binoculars in his bag.

The swing also troubled a camera operator for South African network SuperSport. He had spent a lot of time watching cricket in Durban and had rarely seen a ball reverse so early in such benign conditions. He told the broadcast director, Alvin Naicker, about his doubts.

But perhaps the red flag was in David Warner's left hand. Australia's vice-captain wore heavy bandaging on his thumb, index finger and palm while fielding on day two of the second Test in Port Elizabeth. Some South African batters raised concerns with the umpires about his handling of the ball.

Warner's bandages became a major talking point over the next 48 hours, so much so that his former teammate Ryan Harris appeared on TV to defend him. "The time I played with Davey, he had all that strapping on his fingers," Harris told Channel Nine. "Unless there's something rough – sand or glass or something – on that taping, it's not going to do anything to the ball."

It was 1-1, tensions were running high, and by the time the teams reconvened in Cape Town for the third Test, there would be cameras trained on Australia's every move.

Hatred might be too strong a word. After all, plenty of players on both sides had been teammates in franchise cricket and shared a grudging respect. But Australia and South Africa already had a strained history, and once the series started they became positively hostile.

The friction could be traced back to a bitter three-Test series in 2014 when Australia hit South Africa with "the most abuse we've had on the cricket field", according to AB de Villiers. Dale Steyn had accused the Australians of "bullying" and Du Plessis described them as "a pack of wild dogs". In response, the Australians barked at Du Plessis when he came out to bat.

Then, in 2016, Du Plessis was caught ball-tampering using the fluid from a mint on his tongue. He was fined a full match fee, and South Africa won another fractious series 2-1.

So when Australia touched down in Durban two years later, they did so amid simmering animosity. It boiled over on day four of the first Test when Warner ran out De Villiers for a first-ball duck. Nathan Lyon whipped off the bails before needlessly chucking the ball down on De Villiers lying prone on the ground, while Warner taunted his batting partner Aiden Markram over the crucial wicket.

It signalled Australia's intent to be horrible opponents. Starc and Josh Hazlewood were ruthless with the ball and their teammates were relentless in the middle, chirping away in every batsman's ear. "It annoyed me to such an extent I had to turn my stump mic down," commentator Mike Haysman later recalled.

South Africa were no saints, either. Later that day, as the players left the field for tea, Quinton de Kock allegedly made a derogatory comment about Warner's wife Candice. More than a decade earlier, Candice had been photographed in a toilet cubicle with the New Zealand rugby player Sonny Bill Williams, and their tryst had been the subject of personal barbs. A furious Warner had to be held back in the stairwell to the changing rooms as players from both sides swarmed into the melee, including a half-naked Du Plessis clinging to a towel.

Australia won the first Test by 118 runs. "This series will be one to remember," De Villiers posted on Twitter the next morning.

On day one of the second Test in Port Elizabeth, two Cricket South Africa officials were pictured grinning for photos with a group of fans wearing masks of Bill Williams' face. The Australians were furious – Warner's wife and children were in the stands – and Cricket South Africa was forced to issue an apology.

On the same day, Kagiso Rabada clashed with Steve Smith, shouting in the face of his rival and bumping shoulders after taking his wicket. Rabada was handed a two-match ban, which was later controversially overturned amid feverish debate.

Match referee Jeff Crowe wrote in an ICC report of the incident: "Never in my 14 years of refereeing have I seen such animosity between two teams."

Australia batted first in Cape Town and were bowled out for 255 early on day two. As they took to the field, local camera operators were watching the Australians closely. The bowler, the slips, the man stationed at cover – anyone who handled the ball on its journey back across the field was under surveillance, and soon they honed in on Cameron Bancroft.

There are different accounts of who spotted it first. Commentator Fanie de Villiers claimed he told the SuperSport team: "Have a look, boys. They are using something." At around 2.20pm, one SuperSport operator captured the fatal footage of Bancroft working the ball in his hands. Realising they'd found something seismic, the director Naicker decided to play the replays on his broadcast.

Separately, the Newlands Stadium team put the same footage on the big screen inside the ground. There was no obligation to do so, but they wanted to provoke a reaction with a strategic disclosure of evidence, shaking the tree to see what fell.

The atmosphere quickly turned toxic. Loud jeers filled the air. Australia panicked. Head coach Darren Lehmann got on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb down on the boundary, who dashed onto the field between overs to alert Bancroft.

Realising the grift was up, Smith told Bancroft to stash the sandpaper down his trousers. There was the irrefutable proof, filmed in 150 frames per second: Bancroft gently loosening his drawstring, opening his waistband, pulling the contraband from his pocket and stuffing it inside.

A rare quiet fell across Australia's Fox Sports booth as the team watched the slow-motion replay of Bancroft reaching into his pocket on their TV screens. As his hand emerged, with the yellow flash of sandpaper visible between his fingertips, the realisation of what was happening quickly dawned. "Oh no," came a familiar Melbourne drawl, piercing the silence. Shane Warne was always a beat ahead of the rest.

There was something about the yellow paper, incongruous with the surroundings, conspicuous in its vibrant colour. This was clearly a foreign object, something alien to the cricket field, and the only possible conclusion was that this was not some impromptu gamesmanship but cold-blooded cheating, with a plot and conspirators.

An hour after the close of play, Smith and Bancroft emerged from the Australian changing room to face the music. It was a PR strategy designed to nip the story in the bud, but their obfuscation only made the situation worse. Bancroft claimed he'd used sticky tape and some granules of dirt to rough up the ball, which was a lie. Smith said an unspecified "leadership group" had concocted the plan at lunch. He apologised but insisted he would stay as captain.

Perhaps, had this been just another story of players picking at the seam or applying vaseline to the lacquer, it would have washed away in a week's news cycle. When Du Plessis went through his own tampering scandal in 2014, Smith had spoken up in his defence by insisting such little tricks were commonplace in the game, and it was a relatively brief episode. The South African captain even sent Smith a text message after the events in Cape Town reassuring him that the storm would pass.

But what was so unusual, and gripping, about sandpapergate, was the damning footage of deceit, and of someone clumsily trying to conceal it. When Ben Johnson doped to win Olympic 100m gold in 1988, he was not caught for three days. It took years to bring down Lance Armstrong. Match-fixing scandals and state-sponsored doping require investigations, evidence, hearings, judgements. Whereas Australia were caught in the act, an act beamed to the world in high definition.

And, of course, this wasn't any old village side but the Australian cricket team, an iconic sporting institution as synonymous with greatness as the All Blacks or Brazilian football. In the days that followed there was shock, shame and schadenfreude. Cricket Australia CEO James Sutherland announced an investigation. Prime minister Malcolm Turnbull despaired, saying: "How can our team be engaged in cheating like this? It beggars belief."

The press didn't hold back. The Australian ran the giant headline "Smith's shame" on its front page the next morning. Respected sports writer Patrick Smith lambasted the "earthquake of arrogance" at the epicentre of the scandal. The Darwin tabloid NT News later won an award for its headline: "Why I've got some sticky near my dicky," beside a picture of Bancroft reaching into his trousers.

The overriding question in the aftermath was: who knew? Three days later, once Australia had collapsed to a shambolic defeat, the investigation found Warner was the instigator and he enlisted the young Bancroft to carry out his dirty work. Smith was supposedly the only other person who knew about the plan, and he did nothing to stop it. Cricket Australia banned Bancroft from cricket for nine months; Warner and Smith were banned for 12 months.

Despite global outrage over the incident, they were widely interpreted as harsh punishments, designed largely to show Cricket Australia's strength. There was also the sense that we still didn't know the whole truth. The Australian bowlers really had no idea how their ball was being managed? Experienced fellow cricketers found that hard to believe, but Starc and the rest of the bowling unit have always insisted they were in the dark.

In the closest thing to a clear answer, Bancroft later told the Guardian: "Obviously what I did benefits bowlers and the awareness around that, probably, is self-explanatory." When pressed whether he meant the bowlers knew about the tampering, Bancroft added: "Uh … yeah, look, I think, yeah, I think it's pretty probably self-explanatory."

Australia's back-up spinner on the tour, Jon Holland, recently said Smith, Warner and Bancroft were "hung out to dry".

"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told The Australian. "To Davey's credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it. To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."

Lehmann discovered the scandal with everyone else, as it unfolded on the big screen. The head coach initially stayed on, but later said his family had received such abuse back in Australia that he had no choice but to resign in order to protect them. He wiped away tears as he called on the nation to support his players.

Another burning question remained unanswered: had this happened before? Was this really the only game – the only session, according to Smith – in which Australia tampered? Joe Root was asked whether he suspected they cheated during the Ashes a couple of months earlier and said he didn't think so. In fairness, Australia could have bowled with a tennis ball and still won that series.

Smith and Warner were sent home from South Africa, which led to chaotic scenes at Johannesburg Airport where the captain was mobbed by reporters and photographers. "I felt like I was thrown out to the wolves," Smith later recounted. When he touched down in Sydney, Smith was immediately ushered into a press conference, where he broke down in tears apologising to the nation while his father stood by his side.

Warner's story took a tragic turn days later when Candice suffered a miscarriage. "I was a target right from the start of the tour and I'd have to be bullet-proof for the taunting not to have affected me," she said. "The miscarriage was a ... heartbreaking end to a horror tour."

An ethics committee report, published six months later, blamed a culture of institutional arrogance inside Cricket Australia for creating an environment in which cheating could flourish. "A culture of disrespect for the opposition, as seen in the common practice of abusive sledging, runs through Australian domestic and international cricket, to a degree not practised by other nations," the report concluded. "There is nothing enjoyable or fraternal about abuse. It is simply crude and brutal."

It described a team in which winning superseded everything and senior players were untouchable in their authority. Bancroft desperately wanted their approval and couldn't see beyond the team's win-at-all-costs mentality.

"I invested too much to the point where I lost control of my values," he reflected. "What had become important to me was being liked, being well valued, feeling really important to my teammates, like I was contributing something by using sandpaper on a cricket ball. That's something I don't think I even understood until that mistake happened."

Eight years later, as the Australian Test team finally return to Cape Town later this month, the hierarchy has been replaced. The team culture has evolved. Yet the scandal remains a compelling story, perhaps partly because the plot was so brazen in its simplicity. A scrap of sandpaper was brought on to the field to deviate the ball's trajectory a few degrees, just enough to confound a South African batsman, and instead it sent lives spiralling off-course.

Above all, perhaps the story remains so captivating because it still seems like something of an unsolved mystery. That may change with the passing of time, and perhaps soon: Warner and fellow batsman Usman Khawaja are set to release autobiographies in the coming months that may shine more light on one of the most extraordinary episodes in the history of cricket.

title: 4 players to watch for Oklahoma this week against Texas
description: 4 players to watch for OU-Texas.
fullText:
The Oklahoma Sooners and the Texas Longhorns will renew the annual Red River Rivalry clash on Saturday, and an underdog OU team is far from healthy coming into that game. The initial SEC availability report, released Wednesday night, listed 13 OU players, compared to 4 Texas players. Oklahoma had several players upgraded to probable on Thursday night, but still there's doubt about the availability of two starters for the offensive line.

With all of those injuries, several players will be asked to step up in a big-time environment. Texas is the No. 1 team in the nation, and they'll have no mercy for their arch-rival this weekend. Oklahoma is looking to shock the world, and it'll need some big performances to make that happen.

Here are four players to watch for Oklahoma against Texas.

OU has its two starting cornerbacks healthy for this game: Eli Bowen and Courtland Guillory. However, the third cornerback, Jacobe Johnson, is out with an injury. That means Trystan Haynes will likely a lot more action in Dallas.

Haynes has been part of the backup rotation at cornerback, but he hasn't been on the field a lot so far this season. With Texas' deep rotation of wide receivers, led by Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo, the cornerbacks are going to have their work cut out for them this week. That includes Haynes, in what could be his most significant action as a Sooner.

Oklahoma's offensive line has been banged up this season, and that only got worse over the bye week. Starting left tackle Michael Fasusi (doubtful this week) hasn't played since 12 snaps against UTEP. Now, starting left guard Eddy Pierre-Louis is questionable for this week. Year after year, OU has key injuries up front that they have to work through.

If Fasusi can't go, Ryan Fodje will start at left tackle again. If Pierre-Louis can't play, it'll likely be Heath Ozaeta at left guard. Jake Maikkula is the center, Noah Best should stay at right guard, and E'Marion Harris is again in line to play right tackle.

Other reserves like Caleb Nitta, Peyton Joseph, and Deacon Schmitt could be called upon as well. Ozaeta is a veteran who can play either guard spot, and he is the only player who played a pivotal role during the 2024 debacle that is still left in 2026. Against a very good Texas front line, the offensive line will be under scrutiny this week.

OU's linebackers aren't fully healthy either. While Kip Lewis is off the injury report, Owen Heinecke and Cole Sullivan are probable. That means James Nesta could once again see a larger role.

Nesta has been asked to step up during a myriad of linebacker injuries this season, and he's played a few different spots as the only one of the top four players who has been able to stay fully healthy. He may see some time at Cheetah this week, although Reggie Powers III is still the starter at that position. Still, Nesta's continued growth and relative inexperience will be put to the test on Saturday.

Peyton Bowen, one of OU's starting safeties, has been excellent to begin this season, However, his running mate, Michael Boganowski, still hasn't played since the Michigan game. He was initially listed as questionable against UT but upgraded to probable on Thursday night, so it could be Omarion Robinson starting again in the secondary next to Bowen.

Robinson was expected to be a big part of the safety group this year, but has taken on an even larger role for the last two-and-a-half games. Against Texas, he'll be targeted some, as the least-experienced member of the starting OU defensive backfield. Even if Boganowski plays, Robinson will surely get a steady diet of snaps this week. The Longhorns have a very diverse offense that tricks your eyes, so Robinson has to play well as one of the last lines of defense.

title: Panthers' Bryce Young leaps up NFL QB rankings
description: Bryce Young's sparkling Sunday nighter in Week 4 helped him take a big jump in NFL.com's QB rankings.
fullText:
Heading into the 2026 season, Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young was ranked where he has been most of his NFL career—somewhere between the 25th and 29th best starter in the league. So, this was a major crossroads kind of year coming in—and thus far, Young has aced just about every test with flying colors.

While Young has had better games statistically speaking, last week's performance against the Detroit Lions was the best of his career going by the eyeball test. His command and decision-making were flawless in the face of an obscene amount of pressure.

And now, Young is getting a big boost in NFL.com's quarterback rankings. He's up 12 spots from last week, coming in at No. 9 on the list.

After a rough Week 3, Bryce Young returned to form in Week 4, dicing up Detroit's defense by focusing heavily on throws in the middle third of the field and feasting, even without Jalen Coker. He leads the NFL in passing yards through four weeks and deserves your weekly attention. I can say similar things about C.J. Stroud, who is no longer the problem in Houston.

The only non-excellent start Young has had this season was the loss to Cleveland in Week 3. While he didn't perform well, it wouldn't be fair to put much blame on him given his poor protection and absence of his No. 2 and No. 3 wideouts.

In Young's other three starts, he's been nothing less than brilliant—making the right choices in quick fashion. His processing has largely neutralized what has been the worst pressure rate for any quarterback in the league this year.

Young entered Week 5 with a league-leading 1,268 passing yards along with 10 total touchdowns and two interceptions.

title: Oklahoma vs Texas picks, predictions, odds for Week 6 college football
description: Here are our predictions for Oklahoma's matchup with Texas in the Red River Rivalry on Saturday.
fullText:
NORMAN — Oklahoma faces No. 1 Texas in the annual Red River Rivalry on Saturday at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas.

The Sooners and the Longhorns will meet for the 122nd time. Since 1929, the programs have played annually at Fair Park in Dallas and have played inside the Cotton Bowl every year since 1937.

OU has won five of its last eight meetings against Texas, 11 of the last 17 and 17 of the last 27. But the Sooners are 8.5-point underdogs and coach Brent Venables is at risk of falling to 1-4 against OU's archrival.

The last time the Sooners defeated an AP No. 1 team was in 2007 when OU defeated Missouri, 38-17.

Still, some believe the Sooners can pull off an historic upset. Here are our predictions for this year's game:

More: For OU football coach Brent Venables, pressure 'comes with the territory' against Texas

Sooner defense takes the fight to the Longhorns, but the burnt orange outlasts the crimson and cream late. OU wins the turnover battle (shocking!) but fails to run well enough against the Texas defense.

This is nothing more than a gut feel. Texas is the better team, but we've seen Brent Venables' Sooners come through in must-win games. Remember last November? OU will have a chance so long as John Mateer holds onto the football.

Let's play the old iffin' game at the Cotton Bowl. If John Mateer can match his stats from the Georgia game but not have any turnovers ... if the OU offensive line can overcome Michael Fasusi's absence ... if Isaiah Sategna can break a punt return for a touchdown ... then this OU defense can remind everyone it's elite enough to pull out the win.

OU's defense should match up well against a Texas offense that hasn't been spectacular. The Longhorns rank 102nd nationally in EPA per rush while the Sooners' defense is fifth best in the country in EPA allowed per rush. UT has also committed 19 penalties in its last two games. If OU doesn't turn the ball over, it has a fair shake to shock the country.

Don't expect a lot of points with both elite defenses in this game. That gives the edge to Arch Manning and Co. to again steal a game late with a long drive.

title: Final score predictions for Penn State's Week 6 game vs. USC
description: Penn State welcomes USC to Beaver Stadium for the whiteout game on Saturday night. Will the home field advantage help Penn State? Our staff weighs in.
fullText:
Enthusiasm for the Penn State whiteout game may have fizzled out in recent weeks after Penn State jumped out to an 0-2 record in Big Ten play after last week's debacle against Northwestern, but a primetime game in the national spotlight could be the perfect time for Penn State to reignite the season. Penn State hosts USC on Saturday night as the Trojans make their first visit to Beaver Stadium since 1994 and for the first time as a Big Ten opponent.

The Trojans bring a dangerous offense to the game but are faced with some concerns about the defense. Can Penn State find its offense against the Trojans and pull off a big win against a ranked opponent in the whiteout game?

Here are our final score and player of the game predictions for Penn State's Week 6 game against USC, along with some brief thoughts on the matchup.

The last couple of weeks have set off some serious alarms for me about Penn State, and that does not fill me with a great amount of confidence in the Nittany Lions going into this matchup against USC. The Trojans have struggled with the defense this season but I'm not seeing the firepower necessary to keep things too competitive with the Trojans on Saturdya night. After Northwestern ran all over Penn State's defense, I think the Trojans would be smart to try mimicking that with King Miller setting the tone on the ground and allowing Jayden Maiava to do his thing with the passing game. Kayden Dixon-Wyatt of USC will be a problem all nigth for the Penn State defense.

Final score prediction: USC 27, Penn State 20

Player of the game pick: Jayden Maiava, USC quarterback

This hurts to predict, but I just don't see a way Penn State wins this game. The offense should be able to get back on track against a weaker defense, but if we couldn't stop Northwestern's offense, then I'm terrified to see what USC does.

Final score prediction: USC 38, Penn State 27

Player of the game pick: Chase Sowell, Penn State wide receiver

It feels like the gig is up for the Nittany Lions. What should be a celebration of one of college football's greatest modern traditions could turn into a State College massacre. title: Jorge Martin “struggling” at Mandalika, says Marc Marquez’s pace is “better”
description: Martin couldn’t match his Aprilia team-mates in Practice and remains wary of title rival Marquez at Mandalika
fullText:
Jorge Martin has conceded he "struggled" through Friday practice at the Indonesian Grand Prix despite finishing third-quickest, attributing his difficulties to tyre temperature issues.

As Raul Fernandez set the pace in Practice with a new lap record on the Trackhouse-run Aprilia, factory rider Martin finished a distant third behind the countryman and his team-mate Marco Bezzecchi, facing a 0.481s deficit to the front.

He also trailed behind Bezzecchi in the opening practice of the day, with the Italian edging him out by 0.26s in both sessions.

Although Martin comfortably outpaced his chief title rival Marc Marquez, who has always struggled at Mandalika, the 2024 champion was disappointed with his form in practice, revealing he struggled to get his front tyre up to temperature.

"I had some issues with my front tyre. It was getting cold," he explained.

"I was losing the front everywhere, so I was losing a lot of confidence. I couldn't get into the pace, I was making a lot of mistakes.

"I felt I had speed, but I couldn't put a lot of laps together. When I went into time attack, everything came back to normal with the front. I was happy about that. But I didn't have that extra tool to push for a great lap.

"For sure, I did a good lap, but not amazing. Raul is a step ahead."

Although Bezzecchi was seen as the pre-weekend favourite for victory based on the speed he demonstrated at Mandalika last year, Martin himself has a strong record at the 4.3km track, having won the Indonesian GP with Pramac Ducati in 2024 en route to the title.

Martin is hoping that Aprilia will be able to find a solution for his front tyre problems overnight, having made a similar step in Japan last weekend after struggling on Friday.

"I am far from where I want to be," he admitted. "I feel I was struggling all the practice.

"In the morning, I was feeling super good. I did my last lap, the fastest lap, with really used tyres. But in the evening something changed and I was struggling with the front a lot.

"So I hope to solve that problem for tomorrow. If I am able to solve that and get more confidence, I can be in the fight for sure for the win. But at the moment we are a bit far."'

Martin also remains wary of what Marquez can achieve on the Ducati this weekend, saying he found the reigning champion - who finished two places behind in fifth - to be quicker on long runs.

"Marc is seven tenths off the lead, but only two tenths behind me, so there isn't that much of a gap," he said.

"Obviously, Raúl had a great day today and felt perfect. So now we have the work to do to close the gap.

"But I think Marc is just as good as me, his pace is even better. I knew they were going to work things out and that it wasn't going to be like other years."

Heading into Saturday's sprint, Martin leads the championship by two points over Marquez, with Bezzecchi 49 points adrift in third and the two Trackhouse riders not realistically in the title fight.

Asked whether his Aprilia stablemates were a bigger concern for him than Marquez this weekend, he said "They are always big opponents. Here, it seems like Raul is quite strong, but also Marc is strong.

"We were super close in terms of time attack, super close in terms of pace, in the morning and the evening, so you need to fight all of them. I think Marc will be there, absolutely."
