title: 4 keys to a Commanders' Week 5 victory over the Giants
description: Identifying what the Commanders need to do to get back on the winning track in Week 5.
fullText:
The Washington Commanders are gearing up for their third divisional matchup of the season already in Week 5.

This time, the opponent is the New York Giants. The Commanders already lost to the Eagles and Cowboys, so they desperately need this one this weekend to stay alive.

The good news is that Jayden Daniels is expected to play this weekend. Marcus Mariota went down in Week 4, so the team would have been forced to start third-string passer Athan Kaliakmanis this weekend if Daniels wasn't ready. The Giants are also dealing with quarterback issues, as they'll be without Jaxson Dart for the rest of the season.

Now, let's see what the Commanders need to do to pick up their first division win of the season.

Okay, the Commanders can't totally control how healthy they are, but still. No team can withstand the amount of injuries the Commanders have had, and anybody's depth would be tested at this point.

The Commanders already have Terry McLaurin, Rachaad White, Sam Cosmi, and Nick Cross, among others, dealing with injuries, so they can't afford any more. At full strength, this team can be competitive. This team is definitely good enough to beat the Giants, so let's just hope we don't see any starters go down in the game like we did last weekend.

This is a key every single week because I still haven't been impressed with the Commanders' ground game in 2026. The team is actually near the top of the league in rushing yards per game, but that's mostly because Jayden Daniels has 100 yards.

Bill Croskey-Merritt is averaging under three yards per carry, which just isn't good enough. The Giants are allowing about 110 rushing yards per game, so the Commanders should have chances to run the ball. They need to find consistency, especially with Daniels coming off another injury.

Antonio Williams had a solid NFL debut, catching four passes for 64 yards and one touchdown in Week 1. It's been downhill since then, though, as Williams hasn't had more than 24 yards in a game.

Well, the Commanders may have no choice but to get Williams involved. Neither Stefon Diggs nor Terry McLaurin practiced Thursday, which could leave the receiver room pretty thin once again. What better time than now for Williams to have a career game?

The Commanders and Giants both have a +3 turnover differential so far this season. This means that one turnover could be the difference in this game. The Giants are sticking with Jameis Winston at quarterback, and Winston is one of the most turnover-prone passers in the game.

If the Commanders can make this one of those multiple-turnover Winston games, you have to feel good about their chances. Winston has three interceptions in three games this season.

title: NFL trade deadline: 49ers GM says team is 'always in active mode'

fullText:

That doesn't necessarily mean San Francisco will make a splash before the deadline. Lynch emphasized that teams have to put themselves in a position to make meaningful moves when opportunities arise. With a bevy of injuries at positions like defensive line and receiver, the 49ers could be fits for some players potentially on the trade block. But, that doesn't necessarily mean San Francisco is going to make a deal anytime soon.

The 49ers have already shown why depth could matter. San Francisco is dealing with injuries to several important players, including defensive lineman Nick Bosa and fullback Kyle Juszczyk, while safety Marques Sigle and cornerback Upton Stout are also dealing with injuries. The team has lost several other key contributors on both sides of the ball, like receivers Ricky Pearsall, De'Zhaun Stribling and Demarcus Robinson, as well as defensive lineman Alfred Collins.

There is plenty of time between now and the trade deadline, but it sounds as is the 49ers are at least keeping their eyes and ears open to potential trades that could help bolster their Super Bowl run in 2026.

For a third consecutive year, the Dodgers have advanced to the National League Championship Series. For a second consecutive year, they will be facing the team with the most wins in the regular season, that being the Milwaukee Brewers (again).

The Dodgers lived and died by the long ball throughout the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, with the exception for three runs out of the 14 scored in the four games. None of those blasts was more impactful than Kiké Hernández's two-run home run against Chris Sale in Game 3, as he helped make the difference in a 3-1 victory, helping the Dodgers gain an advantage over Atlanta in Game 4 to close it out.

Hernández continues to shine when it matters the most, becoming the Dodgers' secret assassin in October. His presence in the lineup, based on what he's done in his two games this postseason, is convincing enough for fans to believe in the team's ability to secure a three peat, per Sonja Chen of MLB.com.

"He converts himself into this kind of monster when it comes to the playoffs and when it matters the most," Miguel Rojas said. "He wants the situation. He wants the moment. He wants to be the guy."

Two years ago, Shohei Ohtani suffered a left shoulder subluxation which left him utterly useless at the plate over the final three games of the 2024 World Series. In the end, his lack of production wasn't a drawback that year.

This year, however, represents a different case. Ohtani has not looked like his usual self at the plate, going just 2-13 with two singles and two walks over the four games against the Atlanta Braves. The Dodgers have managed to advance without him hitting like a superstar, but Jack Harris of the California Post wonders just how far the Dodgers can go with him hitting the way he has been since the start of September.

title: Xavi, Laporta pay tribute as Pedro bids farewell to professional career at Camp Nou: ‘Thought about bringing him back…’
description: Pedro Rodriguez brought his remarkable football career to a close with an emotional farewell ceremony attended by several Barcelona legends, including Xavi Hernandez, Sergio Busquets and Carles Puyol....
fullText:
Pedro Rodriguez brought his remarkable football career to a close with an emotional farewell ceremony attended by several Barcelona legends, including Xavi Hernandez, Sergio Busquets and Carles Puyol.

The gathering celebrated his achievements while offering a glimpse of the affection he continues to command at the club he considers home.

Joan Laporta, who was Barcelona president during both Pedro's rise and his later years, also attended the event, where the possibility of a future return to the club emerged as one of the main talking points.

Pedro struggled to hide his emotions as he prepared to address those gathered to celebrate his career.

"I hope I don't get too emotional, but a few tears might fall," he said.

The former Barcelona forward explained that his competitive nature ultimately influenced his decision to retire at 39, believing the time had come to embrace a different chapter of his life.

"The time had come to take a break," Pedro admitted.

"I've always said it: I'm a competitive person and, in the end, I didn't really see myself in that situation anymore.

"After so many teams and so many matches, it was time to step aside and devote myself to a different life," he added.

Reflecting on his journey from a young footballer to an established professional, he said,

"It was a lovely journey. It's always very hard to step out of your comfort zone and leave your homeland. I came here as a child and became an adult."

Although he is ready for life beyond playing, Pedro acknowledged that leaving football will not be easy.

"It's hard to know what to do: I'm going to miss match days, that tension, that passion of playing with a goal in mind.

"I want to enjoy my family and watch my children grow up. But, no doubt, the path ahead will involve football."

Meanwhile, Laporta suggested Barcelona could welcome Pedro back in another capacity, highlighting the importance of maintaining connections with former players.

"We'll see what happens, but I think it's important for the club to bring back figures who have been part of Barça," he began.

"He brings back some great memories: I remember when he made his debut, how he ran after the ball and it was impressive. 'What on earth is this bloke doing?', we thought. He's a fighter.

"I think you call them 'chicharreros'. He'll do well: he's always got a smile on his face."

Xavi revealed that he had considered bringing Pedro back during his first season as Barcelona manager, when the team were going through a difficult period.

"I thought about bringing him back when Dani [Alves] returned – we were going through a difficult patch – but in the end it didn't work out," he noted.

Pedro then recalled his own request to return. "I wanted to score my 100th goal and I said to Xavi: 'Bring me here'."

Xavi spoke warmly about his former teammate's qualities and the work he contributed to Barcelona's success.

"Pedro is a great friend. He's humility personified and it's been a privilege to watch him develop.

"I've never seen him in a bad mood and, in my view, he's greatly underrated by people and in the media.

"For a playmaker like me, the runs he made to get into space, using both feet – he never tired. An incredible player."

Puyol and Busquets echoed similar feelings, stating, "A player you always want to have in your team because he always puts the team first."

Pedro reserved special praise for Pep Guardiola, whom he described as "my footballing father and my great mentor."

"I remember matches where I'd score three goals and he'd tell me I'd been terrible," he recalled.

"Neither of us could ever have imagined achieving what we did. I hope you'll be back soon because football needs you," Guardiola said in a recorded message.

Meanwhile, Pedro also offered advice to the next generation of Barcelona players, drawing on the importance of having a coach who believes in their ability.

"In the world of football, you also need a bit of luck – someone to believe in you, as Guardiola did. If I had to give one piece of advice to the young players at Barça, it would be never to lose heart."

The former forward remains impressed by Barcelona's current generation and believes they can build on the club's previous successes.

"Lamine, Cubarsi, Pedri, Fermin, Gavi… they're playing spectacularly.

"They're performing at a very high level. May they continue to work with this same enthusiasm.

"I think they can follow a similar path. They can even extend our era, and hopefully they can keep playing at this level."

Lastly, messages from former teammates, including Andres Iniesta, Eden Hazard, Sergio Ramos and David Villa, brought the ceremony to a close.

Pedro expressed his satisfaction at ending his career at a club he always considered home.

"It's the perfect ending. My big dream was to retire here, and there was no better way to finish than to be here in front of my fans.

"I may not have been the most high-profile player, but I feel that people have loved me dearly."

Notably, Pedro will take the ceremonial kick-off before Barcelona face Getafe on Saturday, providing one more opportunity for fans to celebrate one of the most underrated players of one of Barcelona's golden generations.

title: Millennial moms saved their American Girl dolls for decades. Gen Alpha has other ideas.
description:
Moms have deep feels about their childhood American Girl dolls — like Kirsten, Samantha and Molly. Passing them down means letting a new generation take the lead.
Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photo: American...
fullText:
Over the summer, I got a text from a cousin whose daughter was almost 7.

"I found a Kirsten American Girl doll on Facebook Marketplace in a town not far from you," she wrote. "I was wondering if you might have a chance to grab it before someone else snags it?"

Her hunt for a vintage Kirsten made by Pleasant Company, before Mattel bought the brand in 1998, had been underway for some time. Her daughter had been saving her lemonade stand profits toward a purchase. Mom had seen a newer version of the doll for sale, but she was holding out.

"I'm finding an OG," she told me.

The retro doll was listed for $90, but she talked the seller down to $75. "This doll exchange is serious business," she told me.

Then came the relay: I picked up Kirsten and drove her home. My husband took the doll on the next leg of its journey, handing her off to one very happy little girl and her mom, who live over an hour away. Three adults and over three hours in the car — all to get one childhood favorite into a new pair of tiny hands.

As American Girl marks its 40th anniversary this year, the girls who once played with the originals are now raising children of their own. Some are taking their old dolls out of storage for them. Others are searching Marketplace and eBay for the Kirstens, Samanthas and Mollys they remember. And then there are those who are buying newly rereleased versions of the historical dolls in stores for the anniversary.

But sharing a cherished childhood favorite means handing it over to someone with their own ideas. Their Gen Alpha kids decide what happens next — swapping Kirsten's prairie dress for a modern outfit, loving Samantha but asking for a pink-and-purple-haired doll for Christmas or packing the dolls away before Mom is ready.

Dorothy Sasso tells Yahoo she was introduced to American Girl by her librarian at age 7. She tore through the historical fiction books that put girls at the center of the story before discovering a postcard advertising the dolls.

"Oh my God, there are dolls!" Sasso, 45, remembers thinking.

Sasso was gifted Samantha for Christmas in 1988 and took her everywhere. An avid reader and future history teacher, she was drawn to the character's rich story: an orphan living with her wealthy grandmother in New York in 1904.

It was mom-approved. Sasso's mother bought herself a Molly, whose story is set during World War II.

At 10, Sasso saved up for Felicity, whose story is set during Colonial Williamsburg circa 1774, and cared meticulously for both dolls. Part of the appeal was the detail of their miniature worlds. Sasso remembers high-quality wooden furniture and ceramic accessories that she treasured and held on to for decades. The dolls even made a cameo in the background of Sasso's wedding day photos.

Launched in 1986 as Pleasant Company, American Girl grew from mail-order catalogs to stores, and the dolls evolved too. Today, historical characters share space with contemporary lookalikes (Truly Me dolls with varied skin tones, eye colors and hair textures), baby dolls, Girl of the Year characters and even Disney princesses.

For children's author and former American Girl magazine editor Aubre Andrus, the attachment goes beyond the dolls themselves.

"They've always taken girlhood seriously," she tells Yahoo. "I just remember feeling so safe and understood, and felt like the things I cared about mattered."

When Sasso's parents sent her childhood American Girl collection to her, she brought it out for her daughters, Claire, now 12, and Audrey, now 10.

"They loved it," she says. But watching little hands playing with the wooden and ceramic accessories made her anxious. "My 3-year-old should not be handling this," she thought. Still, she set up pieces in the kitchen and let them play.

During COVID, they read the historical books chronologically, from Kaya's world in 1764 through Julie's in the 1970s. The girls recognized the outfits and accessories in the illustrations.

"'Wait, you have that in the other room,'" they would say, before running to get the pieces. "'Oh my God, that's from the picture.'"

The first dolls the girls got for themselves were lookalikes. Later, gift cards from their Molly-owning grandmother allowed each of them to choose a historical character as well, making it three generations of American Girl fans.

Sasso then started searching eBay and resale listings for additional historical dolls and older accessories for the girls, entering what she calls a "very thriving buy-sell market." (One seller is asking $2,500 for a set of six original dolls.)

The girls have since packed all the dolls away in the attic, "which was so sad for me," Sasso says. "I was very emotional about it."

She had expected the doll years to last longer, as they had for her. But her daughters are on their own timeline. The dolls still come out now and then — like when Audrey's friends visit — but they're otherwise preserved with Claire and Audrey already imagining passing them down to their own children someday.

Andrus says passing her original Kirsten down to her daughters, ages 8 and 4, comes with a different worry: getting the doll safely from her parents' house in the Midwest to her home in California.

"I'm so precious about her," she says. "If she were to be lost, it would be so sad."

Her daughters already play with Andrus's '90s clothes and accessories. She feels that sharing them means "giving your daughters a piece of girlhood that meant so much to you."

For some families, bringing back that classic piece of childhood means buying new. American Girl's anniversary rereleases offer a route to the historical characters their moms grew up with — with a brand-new box, no musty attic smell and no fear of it going missing during shipping.

American Girl dolls have always been a substantial purchase: In 1986, one with a paperback book cost $68. Today, a rereleased Kirsten with a book and accessories sells for $175.

Influencer Mary Orton Scudellari posted a lighthearted recap of her trip to American Girl Place with her daughters, along with some nostalgic ground rules.

"'You may choose any doll* you want,' I said, gesturing exclusively to the historical dolls," she wrote. She added the footnote, "*Dolls introduced after 1997 are not recognized by this administration, obviously."

She also described her daughters' store visit as "every mother's dream" of "using her children as plausible cover to revisit the defining obsession of her own girlhood."

Other moms' visits take a different comic turn: They arrive picturing their child getting Kit only to go home with Rapunzel.

Andrus says taking her older daughter to American Girl Place to choose her first doll "felt like a rite of passage." She understands why moms are thrilled to "open that door again and be back in that world."

The experience has led the former American Girl magazine editor to campaign to revive the publication, which folded in 2019. Her daughter turning 8 made the mission even more personal. With renewed interest in nostalgia and analog experiences, she believes the timing is right.

"It just feels like this cultural moment," she says. "What strikes me is that people aren't only saying, 'I miss this,' they're saying, 'I want this for my daughter.'"

Kids may be introduced to the dolls through mom, but the play experience — whether the doll is old or new — is all their own.

My cousin was "gutted" when her childhood Molly disappeared during an apparent cleanout of her parents' basement. For her daughter, though, she saw a match in Kirsten: a girl discovering a new world, much like her almost-7-year-old.

But Kirsten didn't have to stay in the 1850s. By summer's end, the doll I'd delivered in her original blue floral dress and apron had a modern wardrobe, including two ice-skating outfits. Mom had introduced the toy. Her daughter decided what came next.

My Yahoo colleague, Kate Murphy, 41, relates. She tells me she saved her childhood dolls, hoping to pass them down someday. During an impromptu visit to American Girl's New York City store last November, she pointed out Kirsten and Samantha to her 6-year-old daughter, Jackie, and asked whether she would like the ones she'd saved.

"Her eyes lit up," Murphy says. The dolls came out of storage in her parents' attic upstate and arrived that Thanksgiving, along with furniture and bedding Murphy's own parents had made for Kirsten.

Jackie enjoys the originals, reports Mom, but the doll at the top of her Christmas list this year has pink and purple hair — her two favorite colors — and eyes that match hers.

"She told me, 'It looks just like me, but I'm just pretending to have purple and pink hair, Mommy,'" Murphy says.

Murphy absolutely loves Jackie's choice, which the girl spotted in a catalog.

"The two dolls belonged to me, and I want her to be able to have a doll of her own that looks like her," she says.

For Murphy, passing down the originals also means letting go of some childhood rules. When she played with the dolls as a child, she never wanted to undo Kirsten's braids or brush out Samantha's hair. So far, Jackie has only been interested in changing their clothes, but Murphy knows that might change.

"I might twinge a bit at first if she decides to brush out their hair, but if that's how she wants to play, let her," she says.

"These dolls belong to her now."

fullText:
PlayStation 5 (version played), Xbox, PC; Epic Games Publishing
This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition

A small band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.

End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.

This combination of cute and eerie immediately marks End of Abyss as part of the Scandi-chiaroscuro style pioneered by Limbo and Inside (from Playdead, in Copenhagen) and Little Nightmares (from Malmö-based Tarsier Studios, where the founders of End of Abyss developer Section 9 cut their teeth). Those games, though, were all puzzle-platformers. End of Abyss is a survival-horror game in the mould of PS1-era Resident Evil, which took a similarly zoomed-out approach, using fixed, CCTV-reminiscent camera angles. It’s a great way of controlling each scene’s composition for maximum aesthetic value – and, of course, to set up scares.

End of Abyss delights in lovingly decorated dioramas, with bodies and viscera laid out just so, illuminated by the flickering light of a CRT screen and some orange-glowing item (a valuable key or weapon upgrade) dangling just out of reach. As you’re studying these details, trying to figure out how you might reach that desirable object, at the edge of your vision a monster will peel itself from the darkness and attack before you can consciously register its presence.

What follows is a dance of backpedalling and firing your pistol, praying that it’s loaded with enough ammo to finish off the advancing assailant before it can catch up to you. Or, worse, your retreat carries you into another nest of monsters. These are foundational thrills of the genre, and End of Abyss keeps them intact as it shrinks them down to dollhouse size. They might be scarier still, in fact, because manually aiming a gun from a top-down perspective can be fiddly, and End of Abyss’s control scheme is so confounding (who puts reload on the right thumbstick?) that you’re fighting muscle memory as much as the monsters.

On top of this survival-horror foundation, though, End of Abyss layers elements of Dark Souls, Metroid and Hollow Knight – and here it overextends. This facility is big and complex enough for you to get lost in, filled with doors that only open from the other side and seemingly separate zones that join up in unexpected ways. These can be some of video games’ finest pleasures, when done right, but they make for an uncomfortable fit in a game that relies on a character so slow-moving that they can be threatened by a shambling zombie.

That striking gloomy style, meanwhile, is something of an achilles heel when you’re trying to tell one room from another. It’s not helped by a pause-screen map that struggles to convey the interlocking territory, and, at the time of playing, is prone to getting confused over questions as fundamental as which doors are locked.

This leads to a lot of unnecessary backtracking and, with every repeat visit, those carefully staged scenes lose some of their sheen. A composition that had you gawping the first time can’t hope to maintain that effect on the dozenth visit, while the shadow-peeling scares turn out to run on the clockwork logic of a fairground ghost train. Reaching the final boss after 12 hours, with much of the map still greyed out and other stretches tromped over endlessly, I’m left feeling exhausted, with little inclination to explore the other half of the game that (according to the completion percentage) remains unseen. Contrary to its fetchingly diminutive presentation, End of Abyss might be just too big for its own good.

End of Abyss is out now; £22.69

title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
description: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled...
fullText:
Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before

OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.

The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.

However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.

Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.

OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.

News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.

The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July.

Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.

Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI.

Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks.

Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race.

Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.

OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn.

Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn.

On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI.

SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported.

Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

title: Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi
description:
AI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other people
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.
“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.
Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?
fullText:
AI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other people

Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.

“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.

Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.

Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put non-toxic glue on pizza so the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.

But culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.

OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. The family’s lawsuit alleges that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)

And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.

Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was probably responsible for the strike.)

In a recent investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.

Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report also adds that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.

AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.

Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.

In September, CNN reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.

Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.

Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.

Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?

And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?

Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?

AI may be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right now. And it’s paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.

Those bad things? They only happen to other people.

Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.

But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.

It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates and bringing us to the brink of world war three because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.

What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. And despite what you may hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.

Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia believe that the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.

Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”

Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”

In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.

 Continue reading...
fullText:
A spokesperson behind the tech company’s AI chatbot has not yet specified what counts as abusive or cruel content

Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.

The Verge first reported the change in policy.

A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”.

In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”.

Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct.

The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare.

“We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website.

The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said he cannot rule out the possibility.

Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea.

“I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Times reported on Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.

fullText:
Donald Trump presented Elon Musk with the top US science medal on Thursday, as the rocket tycoon fully returned to the president's orbit after an explosive bust-up.

Six US tech titans received prestigious awards from the president at a Washington peace institute that was itself recently renamed after Trump.

But all eyes were on trillionaire SpaceX and Tesla boss Musk following his acrimonious departure from Trump's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year.

Trump called Musk a "national treasure" and said that "Elon is our modern-day Thomas Edison," referring to the American inventor of the lightbulb.

"Elon, I want to congratulate you. You're my friend, and all of that, but you are a very, very special guy," Trump added at the summit, dubbed "Science: A New Golden Age.

Along with Musk, Google co-founder Sergei Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD chief Lisa Su all received the National Medal of Science from Trump during the ceremony.

Computer mogul Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella got the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, also the top US award in its field.

Trump and Musk gave an amiable if awkward performance on Thursday, with president patting the tycoon on the back and giving him a wooden case containing his medal. The pair largely avoided eye contact.

It was a far cry from May 2025 when Musk's brief and tempestuous time at DOGE flamed out over his opposition to the White House's "utterly insane" tax and spending bill.

Musk -- the biggest donor to Trump's 2024 presidential campaign -- had spent months working out of a small office in the White House complex as DOGE took a hatchet to the federal workforce and agencies.

He appeared at Trump's side in cabinet meetings and brought his young son X into the Oval Office alongside the president.

After they fell out, relations between the world's most powerful person and its richest person quickly turned bitter.

Trump threatened to deport the South African-born Musk, while Musk, who also owns the X social media platform, alleged links between Trump and late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But Musk has returned to the fold in recent months, and his SpaceX rockets have continued to be a lynchpin of the US space and defense program.

He attended Trump's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September and then joined talks on artificial intelligence at the White House last week.

Musk, Huang and other leaders promised at that meeting to self-regulate against possible threats from artificial intelligence.

Trump has rejected calls for government oversight, dismissing warnings that AI could wipe out humanity and insisting it is crucial for what he calls the "Golden Age" of the US economy in his second term.

Earlier Thursday, Trump said that anyone who does not use the term "super intelligence" -- the term he wants people to use instead of AI -- will be treated as "THE ENEMY."

At the medal event, Trump himself was presented with a frame containing the National Medal of Science posthumously awarded to his late uncle John Trump, a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Trump's uncle, who died in 1983, is a familiar character in Trump's speeches.

The 80-year-old president often says he inherited what he calls the "highest of IQs" from his uncle, citing "good genes."

fullText:
Giant tortoises once pushed to the brink of extinction now outnumber humans in their home of the Seychelles, according to a new survey on one of the African nation’s most remote islands.

The survey, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter in the UK, estimated that about 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll, an Indian Ocean island group off the east coast of mainland Africa.

It is the highest figure ever recorded for the species, and far exceeds the human population of around 122,000 living in the tiny archipelago nation.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild. A much smaller population lives on Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands.

One of the world’s most undisturbed island ecosystems, Aldabra Atoll is home to several unique species that thrive in the remote haven.

The species has rebounded from a dramatic decline. Heavy exploitation during the 19th century reduced its population on the island to fewer than 1,000, pushing the species to the brink of extinction.

A recovery program helped secure strict nature reserve status for the atoll in 1981. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site a year later, giving the population room to rebound.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said in a statement.

“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

Creating the new estimate required more than just a headcount. The figures are based on an analysis of five years of tortoise counts conducted between 2018 and 2022, and is the first update since a widely cited estimate of 100,000 tortoises in the late 1990s.

“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

Bunbury added the team of scientists on the study have produced the most reliable baseline for the species, which can be used as a benchmark to track its population for decades to come.

Despite the encouraging population estimate, the study’s authors said continued vigilance is crucial as the climate crisis brings longer and more frequent droughts that could reduce shade and food for the tortoises. Rising sea levels as the planet warms also threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitat.

The world’s oldest known tortoise, a 194-year-old called Jonathan, is likely to have come from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles.

Guinness World Records lists Jonathan as the oldest living land animal and the oldest tortoise ever. He was believed to be about 50 years old when he was moved to the British Overseas Territory of St. Helena in 1882.

fullText:
Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rain and potentially life-threatening storm surge to the northern Gulf Coast when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday.

The governors of Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared states of emergency, along with several Mississippi counties. Thousands of National Guard soldiers are being deployed.

According to the National Hurricane Center, Isaias is a Category 2 storm with sustained winds of 110 mph. "Isaias is likely to become a major hurricane this morning. Slight weakening is expected before landfall, but it is expected to remain a dangerous hurricane."

The storm could make landfall near the Alabama-Florida state line, though its exact path remains uncertain. Heavy rain and flooding could extend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina through the weekend.

Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Florida's Walton, Escambia, Okaloosa and Franklin counties. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey also ordered nonresidents to evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis urged residents to prepare emergency supplies and "execute your hurricane plan." "Residents should take this storm seriously and evacuate," Okaloosa County officials warned.

Follow live updates on Hurricane Isaias below.

Hurricane Isaias is forecast to make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast tonight or early Saturday

The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties

Hurricane-force winds are expected over areas of the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi

After moving ashore, Isaias is forecast to weaken quickly, becoming a tropical storm over Alabama by early Saturday

A dangerous storm surge combined with the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded

Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia. Flash and urban flooding is likely across the region

Hurricane Isaias has formed as a stronger-than-normal El Niño has suppressed the Atlantic hurricane season.

El Niño is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that forms when weakening trade winds lead to a warming of ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Equatorial Pacific.

It makes it harder for storms to form and strengthen in the Atlantic. Hurricane Isaias, now approaching the northern Gulf Coast, became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914.

El Niño's impact on reducing Atlantic hurricane activity has been linked to increased vertical "wind shear." (Wind shear describes how the wind changes speed and/or direction with height.)

The wind shear pushes the tops and middle of storms sideways, leaving them unable to form the circular eyewall they need to fully strengthen, according to AP.

"Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane ​of the Atlantic season, and ​the very slow and delayed season has indeed been fueled ‌by El Nino-induced wind shear," ​Donald Keeney, agricultural meteorologist ​at Vaisala Weather in Finland, told Reuters.

Hurricane Isaias is strengthening, and preparations should be "rushed to completion" as the weather will "go downhill quickly today," the National Hurricane Center has warned.

In its latest advisory, the NHC shared four key messages for those preparing for the approaching weather:

A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River in Florida. Residents in the warning area are urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate immediately if told to do so.

Damaging hurricane-force winds are expected over parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi. Residents should prepare for potential long-duration power outages.

Damaging wind gusts are possible over much of central and northern Alabama, extreme eastern Mississippi and portions of western and northern Georgia, especially in areas of higher terrain. Residents in these areas should secure loose outdoor items, avoid driving high-profile vehicles and prepare for power outages.

Isaias will bring areas of heavy rainfall to the central U.S. Gulf Coast and much of the Southeast through the weekend. Considerable flash and urban flooding, along with significant river flooding, will be possible.

This graphic based on NOAA data shows the potential track of Hurricane Isaias as it moves north from the Gulf of Mexico.

The image shows Isaias is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane, with winds above 110 mph, before weakening slightly as it nears the Gulf Coast.

It is then forecast to weaken to a tropical storm over Alabama and to a tropical depression as it moves northeast through Tennessee and Kentucky toward West Virginia.

Hurricane Isaias could test FEMA's ability to respond to disasters following significant staffing reductions, according to the Guardian.

More than 4,300 FEMA employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, representing about 17% of its workforce, according to a Government Accountability Office report. The departures included dozens of senior officials, raising concerns about the loss of experienced personnel.

Chris Currie, a director at the Government Accountability Office, told the Guardian, "It's not whether FEMA is going to respond. They're going to respond. It's more about the depth."

Disaster survivors advocate Ginny Goldman described the hurricane as FEMA's "biggest test" since the staffing reductions.

A FEMA spokesperson said, "Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin's leadership, the safety of the American people is DHS's top priority. FEMA incident management assistance teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and FEMA personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. FEMA is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell Air Force Base in Montgomery, Ala., to supplement state resources if requested."

Traffic came to a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, Ala., Thursday, according to videos shared on social media, as residents and visitors prepared for the approaching storm.

Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island.

"Traffic is bumper-to-bumper right now leaving Gulf Shores, Alabama," Jaden Pappenheim wrote on Facebook.

Several Atlantic hurricane names beginning with the letter "I" have been fatal and caused catastrophic damage in recent years.

In 2011, Hurricane Irene sent cars bobbing down rivers, swept away covered bridges, put millions in the dark and killed dozens of people, including six in Vermont.

Category 4 Hurricane Ian in 2022 was the third-costliest storm to hit the U.S., causing $119.6 billion in total, as it wreaked widespread damage across Florida.

But why do hurricanes starting with this letter have such a terrible track record?

Hurricanes starting with "I" typically occur in the middle of June 1-Nov. 30 season, when warming ocean waters can supercharge a storm's energy.

"It's the 'I' storm, which usually we have a lot earlier in the year," Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric and environmental sciences at the University at Albany, told the Associated Press. "It's always the 'I' storms that seem to cause problems."

Isaias is an exception because it has arrived later than usual, in part because the current super El Niño weather pattern has reduced the number of Atlantic hurricanes this season.

Pensacola International Airport in Florida announced it "will close to commercial operations" at 10 a.m. CT on Friday due to the hurricane.

It is unclear when the airport will reopen.

In a statement, the airport said, "Passengers with travel plans during the closure should contact their airlines directly to reschedule their itineraries and confirm the latest flight information.

"Thank you for your patience. Stay safe, Pensacola!"

One Minnesota couple was forced to abandon their planned beach wedding due to Isaias, according to the Pensacola News Journal.

Brooke and Devin Gertken had spent a year planning their wedding in Pensacola Beach, Florida, according to the website, but the approaching storm prevented their friend and officiant from flying in.

The couple instead headed to the Escambia County Courthouse, where they exchanged vows before government offices closed.

"Even though you plan and you did everything that you could, the weather is never probably going to listen to you," Brooke said. "But either way, it's always going to work out, and it's going to probably be better than you imagine it."

Oil and gas production has been impacted by the threat of Hurricane Isaias.

The U.S. Department of the Interior said the Marine Minerals Administration was "monitoring offshore operations and working with operators and state and federal partners."

Chevron and Shell were among the major oil companies to have begun shutting down some oil production sites.

The region accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

About 63% of the oil production in the Gulf had been temporarily halted as of Thursday, according to the Associated Press. The Marine Minerals Administration said 121 of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.

As NBC News reported, the timing of the hurricane compounds an existing issue, with the Iran war already disrupting energy supplies.

A new National Hurricane Center advisory says Hurricane Isaias has strengthened, with maximum sustained winds now at 110 mph, up from 105 mph.

The NHC says tropical storm conditions are expected within 24 hours somewhere in the tropical storm warning areas: the Jefferson-Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Miss., and east of the Bay-Gulf county line to the Aucilla River in Florida.

A tornado risk will begin late Friday afternoon, and continue tonight in the coastal areas of Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and far southwest Georgia, the advisory said. It will continue Saturday across parts of eastern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.

Landfall is expected tonight or early Saturday, with Isaias likely to become a major hurricane this morning before weakening again as it approaches the coast.

Residents boarded up windows as thousands of National Guard soldiers prepared to deploy ahead of Hurricane Isaias.

Coastal communities rushed to prepare as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered nonresidents to evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. According to the Associated Press, traffic backed up on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where beaches were closed to swimmers.

On Dauphin Island, officials also encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly in low-lying areas vulnerable to storm surge. Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, "but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst."

At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, reports NBC Miami ahead of the hurricane.

The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida's Ron DeSantis saying on Thursday about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by today.

"People should take it seriously," he said during a press conference at the state's Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee. "Understand that you are going to have impacts. There's no question."

DeSantis earlier said he would be calling the hurricane "Isaiah," because the word "Isaias" was "weird."

"I'M CALLING IT ISAIAH": Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said he did not know how to pronounce Hurricane Isaias, calling it "weird" during a press conference in Miami. https://t.co/nQXSomL0sZ pic.twitter.com/hoUPNBeLj7

— WFLA NEWS (@WFLA) October 8, 2026

The NHC says short, distinctive names are used to name storms because they make communication quicker and less error-prone. The U.S. started attributing female names to storms in 1953.

According to the latest National Hurricane Center advisory, the following watches and warnings are in place.

A storm surge warning is in effect for the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River, Fla., while a storm surge watch is in effect for the Suwannee River to Yankeetown, Fla.

A hurricane warning is in effect for Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay-Gulf county line in Fla.

And a tropical storm warning is in effect for the Jefferson-Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Miss., and for east of the Bay-Gulf county line to the Aucilla River in Fla.

A hurricane warning means hurricane conditions (sustained winds of 74 mph or higher) are expected somewhere within the warning area, per the NHC. It is typically issued 36 hours before the anticipated arrival of tropical-storm-force winds. "Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion," the NHC said.

A tropical storm warning means tropical storm conditions (sustained winds of 39 to 73 mph) are expected somewhere within the warning area within 36 hours. A storm surge warning means there is a danger of "life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland" — meaning flooding of normally dry land by seawater pushed ashore by the storm — during the next 36 hours.

Residents in Orange Beach, Al. could be seen stocking up on sandbags on Thursday ahead of Isaias's impact.

Sandbags can be an essential part of preparing for a hurricane for many.

According to the University of Florida, 10 sandbags might be sufficient to protect you if your home has suffered minor water intrusion from one or two doorways. However, if your home has experienced flooding from all sides, 10 sandbags will likely not be enough.

The bags should be paired with a heavy-duty plastic sheet and stacked properly — guidance can be found here. Residents should make sure the tarp is higher than the expected flood level and goes underneath the sandbags.

A Category 2 hurricane has extremely dangerous winds between 96 and 110 mph that are projected to cause extensive damage, according to the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale.

While a Category 2 hurricane is dangerous, it is not considered to be a major hurricane on the scale.

Well-constructed frame homes could sustain major roof and siding damage. Many shallowly rooted trees will be snapped or uprooted, potentially blocking numerous roads. Near-total power loss is also expected, with outages potentially several days or even weeks.

Hurricane Isaias is forecast to make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast tonight or early Saturday, with the NHC's tracker (above) indicating it could hit near the border of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle border.

The NHC says landfall could occur on the stretch between Ocean Springs, Miss., and the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida. The storm was in the central Gulf early Friday, about 230 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph. It is moving north-northeast at 14 mph and is expected to turn north later today.

After moving ashore, Isaias is forecast to weaken quickly, becoming a tropical storm over Alabama by early Saturday and a tropical depression by Saturday evening. By Sunday morning, it is expected to be over Tennessee, and by Sunday evening over Kentucky.

title: Former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
description:
— Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.
Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S.
fullText:
OSLO, Norway (AP) — Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.

Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S. President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of the U.N. commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.

Pillay's work "is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world," said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, in announcing her win in Oslo, Norway, as part of the peace prize's 125th anniversary.

The Norwegian committee said it sought to strengthen international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay's award was a message to those seeking to undermine "the international rules-based system and the institutions."

While her career has been global in scope, criticism often has been fiercely local, notably in places like Israel and in apartheid-era South Africa as she and peers took on some of the world's most painful and sensitive legal issues and most vulnerable populations.

Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, the location of the trials of Nazi war criminals that helped lay the foundations of international law.

"Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me," she said to a standing ovation. "You know, you don't want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this."

And, joking, she added: "But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information."

Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the U.N.-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

Gaza was among Pillay's first comments Friday after hearing she had won. "What's happening there is genocide," she said in Germany, to more applause.

The commission last year also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defense minister "have incited the commission of genocide." Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.

Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of antisemitism or allegedly turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel. Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

In an interview with the AP last year, she recalled how she worked closely with some Jewish lawyers in the fight against apartheid in her native South Africa and was invited to Israel as the U.N. rights chief from 2008 to 2014.

The Nobel announcement came at another critical time for Gaza, just two days after the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and sparked the war. Over 74,000 Palestinians have since been killed, with their territory devastated. Saturday marks a year since a fragile ceasefire took effect, while Israeli strikes continue.

A senior Hamas official, Bassem Naim, in a statement Friday called the Nobel for Pillay a message of hope for Palestinians, especially in Gaza, that "humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice."

The Israeli foreign ministry, meanwhile, said in a statement that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner."

It added on X that the award "isn't a recognition of justice. It's the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."

The award also was announced less than three weeks before Israel's election, in which Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power. For Israelis, however, the issue is less about the government's approach to Gaza and more about how well it would protect them from further attacks.

Pillay's win brings renewed attention to Trump's ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was a judge from 2003 to 2008. The Trump administration already has sanctioned 13 of the ICC's staff members, among them key prosecutors and nine judges including the court's Japanese President Tomoko Akane.

In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump called the court an "out of control institution" and an "anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction" over the U.S. as he urged member states to quit the "rogue institution immediately."

There are fears the court as a whole could be sanctioned, a move that could seriously hamper its ability to mete out justice.

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, the highest court of the United Nations, in the ongoing genocide case against Myanmar.

When countries do not have a national on the court's permanent, 15-judge panel, they can appoint an expert of their choice. Gambia, which launched the proceedings in 2019, selected Pillay when the country accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority group.

As a young lawyer in apartheid South Africa, part of Pillay's work involved establishing key rights for political prisoners being held on Robben Island, which included Mandela, who later won the Nobel Peace Prize.

After apartheid ended, then-South African President Mandela appointed Pillay to be the country's first non-white woman to serve as a High Court judge.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year's prize, with just over a quarter of them organizations.

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation.

Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

In Trump's second term, he has been outspoken about his desire for the Nobel, but has expressed doubts that the committee would ever award him the prize.

"They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me," Trump told reporters Wednesday.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week, in the categories of medicine, physics, chemistry and literature. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Dazio reported from Berlin and Keaten from Geneva. Associated Press journalists Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa, Ali Swenson in New York, Cara Anna in Jerusalem, Molly Quell and Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, and Mark Lewis in Stavanger, Norway, contributed to this report.

AP Nobel Prizes: https://apnews.com/hub/nobel-prizes

title: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
description:
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in for an hourlong debate Thursday. (USA Today Network; Reuters; Getty Images)
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping. 
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.
fullText:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.

Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs.

Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks.

“I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point.

Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election.

Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist.

The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly.

“I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.”

Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise.

“It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.”

At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.”

Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump.

New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war.

“I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.”

El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households.

“Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.”

El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”

The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.”

“I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.”

El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer.

“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied.

“We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”

The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts, with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game.

Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith.

Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed. And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”

Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name.

“Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.”

He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.”
