title: What could Rangers' 2012 case tell us about Man City's uncertain future?
description: From sanctions and stripped titles to starting from scratch, BBC Scotland explains how potential consequences for Manchester City compare with the financial collapse of Rangers in 2012.
fullText:
In the wake of Manchester City's unprecedented guilty verdict, the scramble to source similar situations to help shed light on what could come next continues.

But finding a direct comparison has been a struggle because of that very word: unprecedented.

Some have attempted to draw parallels with the demise of Rangers in 2012 as an ominous, dark cloud of uncertainty hangs over the Premier League leaders.

From sanctions and stripped titles to starting from scratch, BBC Scotland explains how potential consequences for City compare with the financial collapse of the Ibrox club and which led to a giant of the British game being dumped at the bottom of the Scottish football ladder.

Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal

Rangers boss McInnes 'not a fan' of extended break

What Guardiola said about Man City charges

It's a long story that, at this stage, doesn't really compare a whole lot to City's.

Rangers' case ultimately became an insolvency event after the club racked up huge tax liabilities. The Employee Benefit Trust (EBT) scheme was a major part of that.

Under former owner Sir David Murray, Rangers paid money into EBTs for employees - including players, managers and directors - for about a decade at the turn of the millennium.

In total, more than £47m came out of the trusts to more than 80 individuals. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) argued the payments should have been taxed as earnings and therefore that Rangers owed substantial sums.

After lengthy court and tribunal proceedings, the Supreme Court definitively ruled in favour of HMRC in its fight with Rangers over the use of EBTs. That came five years after the old company's liquidation.

City, meanwhile, have been found to have arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise more than £830m of funding, according to the Premier League.

The Manchester club have been found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the league's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City have appealed against the verdict and deny any wrongdoing.

With the threat of serious sanctions hanging over City, we wait to find out what comes next.

In Rangers' case, entering administration in February of the 2011-12 season meant a 10-point deduction was triggered. They finished the campaign in second, 20 points behind champions Celtic.

No further penalties were applied, with liquidation ensuing in June 2012.

Rangers were also never stripped of any honours they won during the years they used EBTs, which were ruled to have not gained them "any unfair competitive advantage".

Where things get a bit fiddly, confusing and the source of debate among fans, is the distinction between Rangers the club and Rangers the company.

Following the liquidation, the football assets - including Ibrox, the training ground, name and brand - were acquired by a new company led by Charles Green.

Despite the team continuing to play at Ibrox with the same colours and badge, jibes about Rangers not being the same club are heard from opposing fans at every match.

After Green bought the assets, a vote took place to decide whether Rangers could remain in the top tier. Ten of the 12 top-flight clubs voted against the application, with Kilmarnock abstaining and Rangers voting in favour.

Rangers then had to apply to play in the lower leagues, which at the time were governed by the Scottish Football League, a body separate from the top flight, then called the Scottish Premier League.

This shares similarities with the current set-up in England, with the Premier League separate from the English Football League, which governs the Championship, League One and League Two.

Premier League expulsion has been hypothetically discussed as a potential sanction for City. That could mean they then have to apply to be accepted into the EFL, just as Rangers did with the old SFL.

The Scottish FA recommended Rangers enter the second tier, but that was rejected by the majority of SFL clubs, with 25 of the 30 voting for Rangers to enter the fourth tier instead.

There were fears that without Rangers in the top flight, TV deals would be under threat without Old Firm derbies, putting clubs at financial risk.

Neil Doncaster, the league's chief executive, initially described the reduction in broadcast income as "slight" but acknowledged "there will be money coming out the game as a result of Rangers not being in the top flight".

So what would the loss of Manchester derbies do to the Premier League's?

Then manager Ally McCoist continued in his post following Rangers' demotion and led the team through the fourth and third tiers with relative ease.

The Ibrox icon recently described the 2012 ordeal as an "absolutely horrendous" situation because of the job losses that occurred.

"You're not talking about your centre-forward or centre-back," he said on Talksport. "I had one of the older lads in tears, not a player, just someone who had a wee job, because he was losing his job. It was heartbreaking."

On the pitch, however, McCoist recalled a bizarre but "unbelievable" journey through the lower leagues, hailing the commitment of the fanbase.

"I'll never forget one of the opening games," he added. "We played Brechin and the game got delayed because the ball got stuck on the top of a hedge."

The former striker also said he was dragged off the team bus by the Peterhead chairman to speak to fans in a marquee and did the half-time draw in a social club before his side faced Annan Athletic.

McCoist left midway through Rangers' first Championship season, which ended with them being denied a third straight promotion when they were beaten 6-1 on aggregate by Motherwell in the play-off final.

Mark Warburton arrived in the summer of 2015 and was the man to guide Rangers back to the Premiership.

Just one league title, delivered under Steven Gerrard in 2020-21, has come in the following decade.

Attempting to translate how that would look for City is a challenge given the difference in financial disparity between England and Scotland.

Even in the fourth tier, the budget Rangers were operating with still allowed them to attract some of the Premiership's top talent. That continued throughout their rise through the divisions.

It would be difficult to picture City enticing Premier League players to join them in the event of a severe demotion. And that is before you consider their squad being ripped apart.

Due to the nature of Rangers' plight, they lost a host of integral players without being able to recoup a penny.

The likes of Steven Davis, Steven Naismith and Allan McGregor were among those to lodge objections to a transfer to the 'newco'.

For City, they would at least be able to bring in cash for departing stars, permitting any potential contract clauses.

City fan Matt Mellor joked he "can't wait to see Erling Haaland bag a hat-trick against Grimsby" in League Two next season. McCoist isn't convinced.

"When you go down there, you're effectively starting from scratch, because the players won't stay," the Rangers great said.

"If you're talking about Manchester City, you're starting again. You're officially starting again."

title: Wales captain James has World Cup on her mind
description: Wales take on Albania over two legs in the semi-finals of the play-offs motivated by reaching a World Cup for the first time.
fullText:
Captain Angharad James says the Women's World Cup is always on her mind as Wales prepare for Friday's play-off semi-final first leg in Albania.

Wales' women look to take a step closer to a first World Cup appearance in the nation's history as they face the Albanians in Shkoder.

Rhian Wilkinson's side will have home advantage in next Tuesday's return leg at Parc y Scarlets with the winners facing either Norway or Romania in a two-legged play-off final in December.

Even if they come through both play-off rounds, Wales may then have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs in February to book their place at next year's tournament in Brazil.

Yet James, 32, says she is already thinking about the idea of representing Wales at the World Cup during "every training session, every day".

"It's always in the back of my mind," the Seattle Reign midfielder added.

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"I've always wanted to play in a World Cup and I think if you ask the majority of the group, the way we turn up and train and play every day for [our] club is for moments like this with our national team.

"Every day I'll make sure I do extras. I do everything that I can to best prepare myself and the team to reach the first World Cup."

James was a central part of the squad who ended Wales' wait for a women's major championship appearance by qualifying for Euro 2025.

As they look to make it two tournaments in succession, Wilkinson's players did all they could during the group stage of World Cup qualifying by topping Group B4.

But with no automatic qualification route available to teams in League B, Wales face a demanding play-off process which begins in Albania.

Even with their squad depleted by injury, Wales will expect to overcome the Albanians, who they beat twice in the group phase.

But a probable play-off final against Norway – with the second leg away from home – would be a far sterner challenge.

Even so, James says Wales have the "strength and depth" required to carry them to a World Cup.

"We know it's not an easy road ahead of us," she added.

"It's a big challenge. We've got a big game [in Albania], we've got big games ahead of us and the road is never easy.

"But it's one that I truly believe this group can get through. With the help of the staff and the whole squad, we can achieve big things and reaching the World Cup would be the biggest honour."

Wales eye shutout in World Cup play-off first leg

Wales focus on Albania as Grainger reunion looms

Wales' injury worries deepen as duo withdraw

Should they overcome Albania – and Norway beat Romania - Wales will turn their attention to a reunion with Gemma Grainger.

The Englishwoman, who came close to guiding Wales to the 2023 World Cup, stepped down as Welsh boss in January 2024 to take charge of Norway.

Upsetting Grainger's Norway, who are ranked 14th in the world, would be a major coup for Wales – and yet at this stage, Wilkinson's squad do not know if that would be enough to seal a World Cup place.

There will be eight European play-off winners, with seven progressing straight to Brazil and one – the lowest-ranked nation from the group stage of qualifying – going into inter-confederation play-offs next February.

James says she would like to see the qualification process changed in the future.

"You play a final and you could win the final and still not reach the World Cup," she said.

"So as players, do you celebrate that moment, do you not? It's mixed emotions, but hopefully the pathway will change in the near future."

title: What to do with Joao Pedro? FPL gameweek six dilemmas
description: BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert FPL Pras gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers in gameweek six.
fullText:
BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert Pras gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek six.

Despite being the most sold player of the international break, Chelsea forward Pedro is still owned by about 65% of FPL managers. From a points-per-million point of view he remains one of the best picks in the game, and Chelsea's fixture run is excellent for a long stretch. Unless manager Xabi Alonso rules him out completely, I would hold and use the bench.

This is a tough week for captaincy. Erling Haaland is away at Liverpool. Cole Palmer is home to Bournemouth. Bukayo Saka has the Saturday lunchtime kick-off at home to Leeds. Bruno Fernandes is at home to Spurs.

Fernandes has the best fixture and the best chance of a big score, but not many own him. Of the rest, you can talk me into any of them. I am leaning safe and sticking with Haaland. Even in a tougher game, if Man City score he should be the one involved.

If I wanted to be different, I would look at Saka or Palmer, both at home. What puts me off Saka is the possible Havertz injury that will impact their attack, plus an early kick-off straight after a long break. What puts me off Palmer is Joao Pedro. If he is not fit, the Chelsea attack suffers, as we saw in gameweek five against Brentford.

For a new buy, yes. The Arsenal defender has a slight niggle from the England camp. Cristhian Mosquera is fit, and William Saliba is on the mend as well, albeit with an unclear timescale for his return. I would not sell him if I already owned him though - he still represents excellent value.

On a wildcard, or with a free transfer though, there are better defenders in the £5m price bracket, in my opinion.

Fulham play all three promoted sides in the next three games. Gonzalo Garcia at £6m is the one I like. He may be on penalties, and the underlying numbers have been better than the FPL returns suggest. Josh King is the other option. His data (0.44 xGI) is strong and the minutes have been good with 90 minutes in three of the first five games.

Not an urgent sell, although there are concerns there from an FPL point of view with his role.

Under Andoni Iraola he is playing as an eight, not as a 10, and not at right-back. That is the worst of the three for route to points. No real attacking threat from the 10 spot, no defensive contribution from full-back. What is left is set pieces and the odd shot from outside the box. I would not rush him out though.

Close to it, at the price. The Brighton midfielder is still under £6m, he plays 90 minutes, and 47 points already explains why he is the most-transferred player this week.

Ownership is about 30%. Sunderland away, then Crystal Palace at home, is a decent run of fixtures. He is just an easy set-and-forget midfielder who keeps playing 90 minutes and keeps trickling points in.

Aoife Wafer has been ruled out of Ireland's WXV Global Series trip to South Africa later this month.

The two-time Women's Six Nations player of the tournament missed Ireland's back-to-back wins over Japan in Galway and Cork after sustaining what the Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) called a "minor injury in training".

However, the 23-year-old Harlequins player will not travel with head coach Scott Bemand's 30-player squad for the WXV contests against the Springbok Women in Cape Town on 24 and 31 October.

Former co-captain Sam Monaghan remains unavailable with an Achilles injury but second row Ruth Campbell returns from an ankle injury to make the squad.

The squad, led by captain Erin King, includes recently capped players Beth Buttimer, Jemima Adams Verling, Kate Jordan, Sophie Barrett and Alana McInerney.

Following a remote training week after the wins over Japan, the Ireland squad will return to the IRFU High Performance Centre on Monday before travelling to Cape Town on Thursday.

Ireland's only previous meeting with South Africa was a 2006 Women's Rugby World Cup match in Canada, which the Irish won 37-0.

title: EFL preview: Savage salvation and a happy homecoming?
description: Here are the five things across the EFL that you should be keeping your eyes on this weekend.
fullText:
It takes two weeks inside a chrysalis for a butterfly to emerge, eye-catching in flight, but could the same metamorphosis happen for a football team?

Not all of the English Football League have enjoyed a fortnight off during the international break; teams in League One and League Two have continued their campaigns while a number of players have been off representing their countries.

However, October still offers a fresh start. Close enough to the start of the season for new managers to make an impact in the league, far enough that sides should be finding their footing.

Here are some of the standout fixtures and narratives across the EFL that you should be keeping your eyes on this weekend.

West Bromwich Albion defender Conor Townsend labelled their 1-0 loss to local rivals Wolverhampton Wanderers their "worst performance of the season" but a chance to show they can turn up in a big match has rolled around quickly.

The Baggies return to action with yet more bragging rights on offer, this time welcoming Birmingham City to The Hawthorns on Saturday lunchtime (12:30 BST).

Like Wolves before them, Blues could leapfrog their hosts on the table should they take victory and Albion will be keen to stop allowing their West Midlands foes from using them as a stepping stone closer to the top.

Last season though, the two shared the points in both Championship fixtures with just one goal each - and it was not the only derby to be so tight.

The South Coast meetings between Southampton and Portsmouth last season carried high expectation but both games fell a little flat. In fact, the teams have drawn four of their past five meetings.

Saints may feel a little buoyed this time around though when they meet at St Mary's on Sunday (12:00 BST).

Spygate is finally behind them after boss Tonda Eckert was given a six-week suspended ban for his role in the controversy by the FA.

Portsmouth are on a three match unbeaten run and will be hoping that the media spectacle of Eckert's punishment can prove a suitable distraction for their opponents from the true prize - local pride.

Eckert "got off very, very lightly" - McAnuff

Hellberg reveals Eckert apology after Spygate

'Thank you for support' - Saints boss Eckert speaking to media

Steven Schumacher left a promoted and thriving Plymouth Argyle to head north to the Bet365 Stadium in December 2023, only to be sacked in September after 32 games.

But, despite the knockback, Schumacher is back in the Championship after leading Bolton to promotion and the Trotters have shown they have plenty of fight in them.

Three of their four losses have been by the margin of a single goal and they have won their past two games to be just three points short of the play-off positions.

His former employers will represent a tough challenge on Saturday (15:00 BST) though with Stoke on a five match undefeated run (W4 D1) and looking to keep consolidating their goal of being a promotion contender.

"At Stoke there has been lots of change, they've moved managers on, they've tried these winning formulas," former Nottingham Forest and Ipswich Town defender Luke Chambers told the 72+ podcast.

"But with Mark Robins, he's a fabulous manager. Stoke City have impressed me, especially within the past few weeks."

Schumacher happy with Bolton points tally

Graham Alexander is much loved at Deepdale from his playing days, where he made 410 appearances and became club captain.

Fourteen years after his retirement, he is back at the club he claims is "special" to him and with a mammoth challenge on his hands.

The Lilywhites are kept off the bottom spot on the Championship table by just one goal and have managed a solitary win so far this season.

Next they face Millwall on Saturday (15:00 BST), a team that have been beleaguered with injuries but still just two points off the play-off positions.

Preston return 'surreal' and 'special' - Alexander

Alexander wants a winning atmosphere at Preston

Duff at ease with expectation in Bradford role

Conversely, Bradford City will be aiming to show their recent successes have come from more than just possessing Alexander in charge.

Alexander led the Bantams to promotion in 2025 plus a play-off semi-final last season before losing to eventual winners Bolton.

The former Scotland international has left them in pretty good stead too, second on the table level on points with League One leaders Plymouth Argyle.

The man in charge of making sure they continue where they left off is Michael Duff, the former Wycombe Wanderers boss with some big boots to fill.

Duff isn't concerned about the eyes on him though as he prepares for his first game at the helm against Leyton Orient on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"I'm under no illusions, they [the owners] will let you know [if you're doing a bad job]," Duff told the 72+ podcast.

"I like the fact they will because there is an expectancy. It's a big football club. I'd rather have that pressure than playing in front of 200 people that don't care if you win or not."

Robbie Savage has undertaken a huge task in leading Peterborough United away from the bottom side of the table - but it's already got off to a good start.

Posh scored four times in less than 10 minutes for Savage's first game in charge, a 4-1 victory over Ipswich Town in the EFL Trophy.

It brings back times of yore for the club, renowned for their attacking prowess but finding themselves lacking this season as the lowest scorers in League One with just four goals in eight games.

Savage wants Peterborough 'mentality' shift

Savage's first chance to make an impression in the third division - and the EFL in general for that matter - is against former club Leicester City, where he made 204 appearances as a player across a five-year stint.

"He is box office, isn't he?" former Middlesbrough defender Tommy Smith told the 72+ podcast. "But he's got a tough start. Three of his next four are away from home. He's got Leicester on Saturday, he's then got Huddersfield and also Bromley."

The two sides meet on Saturday (15:00 BST) and while Russell Martin is still struggling to win over hearts at mind at the King Power Stadium, the Foxes league form has shown some signs of life with a win over Stockport and a draw at Barnsley leading into this fixture.

Things are going mighty well for Salford City and Cheltenham Town as of late.

After three successive losses to open their campaign in August, the Ammies' turnaround to rise to the top spot has earned boss Peter Cklamovski the manager of the month award for September.

Meanwhile, Cheltenham have only lost two games and midfielder Charlie McCann has shown so much influence in the middle of the park that he was named player of the month.

But awards mean nothing if they can't keep the results flowing.

The two meet on the Robins' home turf on Saturday (15:00 BST) and if they win and things go in their favour elsewhere, they could be snatching away Salford's place at the apex.

title: 'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'
description: Northern Ireland striker Simone Magill tells BBC Sport NI about balancing motherhood with her return to football and how her life has changed since giving birth to daughter Skye earlier this year.
fullText:
"Football will always be a large part of my life but it's very much what I do, not who I am.

"Ultimately, I'm Skye's mum and, to me, that's the most important thing."

Through her 16-year footballing career, Simone Magill has been something of a trailblazer in Northern Ireland.

From a senior debut at the age of 15, helping the country to a major tournament debut and becoming captain, she has been there and seen it all.

But after giving birth to her first child, Skye, in May, her focus is paving the way off the pitch, as well as on it.

"I think we get labelled as athletes, and that is our complete entire identity," Birmingham City striker Magill told BBC Sport.

"Obviously there's been a massive shift now. I'm a mum first and foremost and that is the highest title that I will ever have.

"Family is so important. It's my priority, and it's so nice for me to have that greater purpose now.

"It's hard and it can be overwhelming, but it's the greatest joy that I've ever experienced in my life."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil

Magill is speaking at the Northern Ireland camp in the lead up to Friday's World Cup play-off with Portugal.

While she is stepping up her training four months on from giving birth, the first round of play-offs have come too soon.

However, after conversations with manager Michael McArdle, who has spoken about the importance of family, the 31-year-old is in camp to train with the squad.

More importantly, Skye and her husband, Mark, are with her for the duration.

It is a glimpse into what the future will look like when Magill is back playing for Northern Ireland.

"It's so different, but it's so special. I'm really enjoying being back in, and I think I find it weirder having my husband here than having Skye," she said.

"It's just amazing that I'm able to do this and the support that I've been given to allow me to do this has made things so much easier."

After nearly a year away from the squad, from when she announced her pregnancy last November, she says the support that the Irish FA and her Northern Ireland team-mates have provided has meant "I don't need to worry about anything".

Skye and Mark have become fully integrated in the camp and join the team for meals and in downtime.

Then, when it comes to on-pitch matters and meetings, Mark is able to look after Skye and Magill can focus on the football side of things.

"Mark has his daddy-daughter days with her while I'm on the training pitch.

"Then when I'm here with the girls in and around the hotel and free times, we're all here mingling with Skye.

"She's now got 23 aunties who are all very hands-on."

Before camp, Magill admits there was a bit of apprehension about how integrating back into the group with Skye may look, but "I feel a sense of obligation to pave the way".

While she is not the first Northern Ireland player to have a child and return to playing - experienced defender Sarah McFadden gave birth to her second child in 2024 - Magill is the first to have the family integrated into the camp.

"So it's the unknown of what things are going to look like," she said.

"It's relatively new in the game and I suppose I'm one of the first people certainly here and at club as well to do this.

"There are going to be certain things that we might need a little bit more support with, but we don't know that until we go through each phase and we're navigating that all collaboratively."

Magill feels that having Skye with the group is "lovely for the mood" and "gets everyone involved" as the new arrival is the most popular member of the camp.

She added that having Skye and Mark in camp has been "game-changing", and pointed to how a new mother in a more traditional job would have a year off, while her career means she is looking to get back on the pitch as quick as possible.

"If I didn't have that support then it almost questions, 'can I still play football if I can't bring her?'

"But it means that I can fully focus on being a footballer, but equally put everything into still being a mum at the same time."

While Skye has yet to be given a club team to support - Magill has played for Everton and Aston Villa before joining Birmingham and Mark supports Manchester United - there is no debate surrounding her international allegiance.

Despite Mark being from England, Skye has already been decked out in a mini-Northern Ireland kit.

"It's so important for me that she can come back to Northern Ireland often and just be surrounded by Northern Irish accents, to show her where I've come from and my roots. It's really special."

Magill said that she and Mark, who got married in 2021 after meeting at university, had always wanted to start a family and "we almost had to remove football from that decision".

While she stopped playing matches when she found out she was expecting, she was still active in training and the gym right up to a few weeks before Skye was born.

Just four weeks after her arrival, Magill was back doing gym work and she was back on the pitch after 13 weeks.

Now fully training again, she hopes to be back playing matches later in the autumn.

"It's funny because when I announced my pregnancy, I think the natural assumption from a lot of people in the scope of wider things thought that that was probably going to be the end of my football career.

"But I was like, 'well, no, absolutely not'.

"I very much wanted to be a voice and showcase that you can be a mum and a footballer, and those things can both co-exist."

Magill has spent longer away from playing matches than when she sustained an ACL injury at Euro 2022, but the stresses of rehab are absent.

For Magill, Skye has given her a new drive and purpose. Only five games away from a century of international caps, she dreams of walking out onto the pitch with her in her arms.

"Skye will not necessarily remember any of this, but I will.

"When she's older she can look back and see the hard work that I put in to come back and play, and it was all for her.

"All throughout my pregnancy I was almost manifesting that moment that when I make my return and being able to carry her out onto the pitch, I think, you know, that's what's driving me."

Magill said that McFadden was a role model for her when it came to balancing family and football, and now she wants to inspire other players to take the same step.

"We have a lot of younger members in the squad now and hopefully it is a very normal thing for them to see that this can be done.

"You know that there's a player playing for the team that has a child and she's able to bring the child in.

"That's very important to be normalised now in our sport and I'm just so thankful that the support systems are in place to allow me to do this.

"I've always wanted to inspire people on the pitch, but hopefully this is something I've done off the pitch that could also inspire future generations to show that it's possible."

title: Maresca will be demanding a siege mentality from Man City - Pulis
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains why Manchester City players have a great chance to show unity and togetherness when they travel to Anfield on Sunday.
fullText:
If I was manager of Manchester City now, after they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules, my whole psychology with my group of players this week would encompass one major point:

"No-one is going to like us, but we won't care."

I loved being the underdog and I loved to prove people wrong, and that is what I would demand now - a siege mentality from my squad and supporters alike to prove to people that, irrespective of what is happening off the pitch, on the field and the terraces we respect our club and we are going to fight on.

City will be vilified by everyone else but their players have a great opportunity to show unity and togetherness, starting on Sunday away to Liverpool.

When the Premier League returns this weekend, the spotlight will be on one game in particular - at Anfield.

As well as preparing for such a huge match, City's players will be arriving back from international duty and going straight into an off-field fight that has turned into a media frenzy.

The allegations seem relentless with finger-pointing from every Tom, Dick and Harry jumping on the bandwagon in hammering a club that has dominated the Premier League for over a decade.

It feels like every positive gained by City over the period in question and beyond has been smashed into oblivion. Yet, despite all of the above, the club have remained firm in denying all charges.

So, where does this leave Enzo Maresca and his City players as they prepare to take on Liverpool?

Firstly, although they themselves have not been involved in any of the allegations about the club breaking the Premier League's financial rules, they must understand that supporters at all away grounds will be baying for their blood.

City have become a team that, whenever they play, will provide an opportunity for all critics to attack them, and from all angles - including the frenzied media outlets.

So, as the manager, Maresca must first act to reassure his players that the club is not in any way going to take a step back from defending their own position, and also the position of the players, staff and supporters.

Once that is established, I would then expect every player to concentrate on what they are being paid for, which is to win games.

There should be no distractions or any questions that do not relate to the games they are involved in. No excuses about what is happening off the field would be tolerated, and that would be my final word on the matter.

If the verdict about City breaking the Premier League's financial rules is upheld, it will come at a heavy cost to the club and its reputation.

I feel there needs to be more attention paid to all of these rules, and their fairness, because professional football at the top level is now dominated by massive financial investment.

Even if you just consider player transfers, it's not unusual for around a billion pounds to be exchanged between clubs in England and around the world during each transfer window.

While individual players at the top level are being bought and sold for more than £100m, smaller academies are being plundered by the bigger clubs.

They can hoover up the best young players for much smaller 'compensation' fees, enabling them to polish them up and sell them on later for much more - without any Financial Fair Play rules to regulate how much they profit.

That's one way of dealing with FFP, I suppose, but is it for the good of the game, or the players involved?

Over many years of Premier League governance, clubs have broken the FFP rules that are in place. Some have not been caught yet, I'm sure, but others have and have been punished. It keeps happening, so are the current rules right?

Do we need to try to change them or are we taking a bigger risk by leading clubs to find different ways - or loopholes - to try to break the financial shackles that are currently in place?

The money in our game today is extraordinary and today massive corporations, billionaires and even countries are buying our clubs and want to invest more and more into the product but are not able to.

Gone are the days of local business owners buying their local clubs.

In the Premier League, Tony Bloom at Brighton and Matthew Benham at Brentford are the last men standing and, in the Championship, the Coates family at Stoke City and Steve Gibson at Middlesbrough are among the few to have had a taste of the top flight.

I always see the top clubs having the power financially to remain at the top but it's important there is a way for the smart guys - people like those I named above - at clubs without the big bucks or big histories, to play a leading role in the top league in world football.

At the moment all the negative media attention is on what Manchester City have done wrong but the likes of Brighton, Bournemouth and Brentford have achieved success by being smart, without the 'big club' tag.

It's great to see, but surely the rules need to reward all clubs for being smart. Doing the right thing should give everyone the chance to compete at the highest level.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

title: ECB help would make women's Test a 'certainty' - West Indies
description: West Indies are still hopeful of hosting England in a women's Test next year, but the fixture would be a "certainty" if the ECB were to help fund it, says chief executive Chris Dehring.
fullText:
West Indies are still hopeful of hosting England in a women's Test next year, but the landmark fixture would be a "certainty" if the England and Wales Cricket Board were to help fund it, says chief executive Chris Dehring.

ECB chair Richard Thompson suggested on Monday the board could step in to help the hosts, who have recently revealed significant financial pressures, to maintain the red-ball element of the multi-format tour.

England, in part at least, want the Test to go ahead to aid their preparations for next summer's Ashes while it will be a first women's Test for West Indies since 2004.

"We would welcome any assistance of our much wealthier member boards," Dehring told BBC Sport.

"It is very expensive to host cricket in Caribbean."

ECB may fund women's Windies Test to aid Ashes preparation

Cricket tours often involve reciprocal arrangements between boards over costs. They usually mean the home board pick up the logistical expenses of the visitors, including things like travel and accommodation.

In the West Indies, costs can be inflated by the need to fly players and officials between islands.

Cricket West Indies is also hurt by the cost of the TV production. It announced a wide range of money-saving measures, including cuts to player contracts last week.

"We have to fly all of the equipment and crew into any venue to be able to broadcast a match," Dehring said. "That is a significant figure.

"Sky doesn't have to fly from London to Manchester for one match."

West Indies, who cancelled a women's Test against Australia earlier this year, are yet to announce a schedule for the England tour, which is due to be played in April and May next year and includes three T20s and three one-day internationals in addition to the Test.

The process in which islands bid to host the next block of home fixtures began in recent days and should conclude in December.

Dehring said there has been interest shown in hosting the women's matches.

"Once we develop a schedule we will know how much it will cost," he added.

"It is far cheaper to host everything in one location but one of the allures of the Caribbean being able to travel to more than one location for matches.

"We are hoping still we will be able to cover from our own resources but it [the Test] would be a certainty if the ECB were to assist us."

title: UFC fighters aren't paid enough to retire, says Strickland
description: Sean Strickland says UFC fighters are not paid enough money to retire from the sport on their own terms.
fullText:
Sean Strickland says UFC fighters are not paid enough money to retire from the sport on their own terms.

The 35-year-old middleweight champion criticised the promotion earlier this week, saying his "heart isn't in MMA anymore" after injuries to his groin and shoulder.

Strickland added he would prefer a move to boxing, citing the sport as "significantly easier" with "more money" to be made, before calling for a fight with Jake Paul.

Following up his comments in a post on Instagram, the American says fighters are ruining their legacies by having to fight on for money instead of walking away from the UFC.

"I'm going to say the quiet part out loud that nobody says. You watch these champions, they run the division and they take [a loss], and then they come back and they fight three or four times and get flatlined," said Strickland.

"You're like, 'dude, what happened to you?' And you realise the UFC happened. They just don't care anymore.

"They don't pay you enough money to walk away. The UFC builds a legacy and they don't pay you enough. So you have to come back and ruin your legacy. I don't want to do that."

Former UFC security guard Everett wins fighter contract

'Unfinished business' - Coker's bid to shake up MMA

Fighter pay has been questioned by athletes and the media this year after boxer Conor Benn signed a reported £11m one-fight deal with Zuffa Boxing.

Zuffa Boxing is owned by UFC president Dana White, so critics have asked why the 57-year-old isn't paying similar amounts to his MMA fighters under contract.

When asked about criticisms amid the Benn deal, White said "it's a good thing" when people make more money and pointed to fighter pay continuously rising since 2001.

White referenced the UFC's new £5.7bn broadcast deal with Paramount, before adding: "I promise you fighter pay is going to be just fine over the next seven years."

The UFC gives about 20% of revenue to fighter pay, compared with boxers who get about 60% of revenue from their events.

Fighters can't compete under other major promotions while in contract with the UFC - a clause which Strickland has criticised.

"I want to box. I want to go win a boxing title. So we're trying to work that out," added Strickland.

"But if the UFC says, 'hey, we're not going to do that. We're going to make you fight.' Well, I'm going to stick and move, and you guys will boo and I'll boo while doing it.

"Just stick and move, collect my check, and then move on. But I mean, hell, here we are."

Strickland is a polarising figure in MMA and has made homophobic and racist remarks as well as derogatory comments about women.

He became a two-time UFC middleweight champion by beating Khamzat Chimaev in May.

title: In-form Carpenter aims to advance England case by outshining Furbank
description: In-form Sale full-back Joe Carpenter admits part of him is focused on outshining Harlequins' George Furbank this weekend to advance his case for an England recall.
fullText:
In-form Sale full-back Joe Carpenter admits part of him is focused on outshining Harlequins' George Furbank this weekend in an attempt to force his way back into the England reckoning.

Only Exeter wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso has beaten more defenders in the first two rounds of the Prem this season, as Carpenter has shown a keen attacking edge.

Furbank was England's first-choice full-back this summer before an appendicitis sidelined him for last summer's Nations Championship, while Carpenter has not been involved in Steve Borthwick's set-up since winning his only Test cap in a 40-5 win over the United States in July 2025.

Their two sides meet at Sale's Corpacq Stadium on Sunday, with Quins looking for their first points of a miserable campaign so far.

"Yeah I'd say so, in a certain aspect," said Carpenter when asked if the personal duel with Furbank was motivation.

"Those boys [Harlequins] have just come off the back of a pretty big loss and they'll be emotionally spiked come this weekend.

"So yeah it would be nice to have a very good performance against them and against that England competition"

Carpenter, who also scored a hat-trick of tries against Bath in the Prem Cup last month, partly puts his fast start to the season down to missing out on England selection.

After touring Japan and New Zealand in 2024 and Argentina and the United States in 2025, Carpenter's absence from a gruelling long-haul Nations Championship trip enabled him to take part in a full club pre-season for the first time in three years.

"Those summer tours are very intense - training's competitive, the games even more so - so to miss out on that was unfortunate," Carpenter added.

"But to actually get a full 10 weeks of pre-season and preparation, getting the body right, was definitely something I needed. I think it's shown in spades really from the games, I feel a lot fitter and a lot stronger.

"I'm just probably outside the mix [for England] at the moment but having back-to-back performances and playing as well as possible will definitely put me in the best position to hopefully get involved come November."

England coaches have challenged Carpenter to improve his decision-making in backfield and his stamina to cover ground and repeatedly take on tacklers. He scored highly in Sale's fitness testing when he reported for pre-season and has been an elusive threat with ball in hand.

"Beating defenders is a massive part of my game," he added.

"But that repeatability is massive and something that I'm definitely feeling the benefits of, being able to go again and again and again at speed.

"It is putting me in better positions and giving me more opportunities to not only just get the ball, but affect the play positively when I do."

Carpenter admitted that, after reaching the play-offs in each of his previous three seasons at the club, a disappointing seventh-place finish in Sale's last campaign gave him pause for thought before he signed a new deal with the club this summer.

Sale won only five of their 18 league matches in the league and were on the wrong end of an 85-19 drubbing by Saracens in April. They were also comfortably beaten by Leinster in the last eight of the Champions Cup.

However, coach Alex Sanderson has been backed, with former England captain Courtney Lawes heading a clutch of new signings.

Lawes, backed up by the experienced Tom Curry and George Ford, produced a fine performance as Sharks claimed only their second-ever league win away to Saracens last weekend.

"After last season, re-signing was probably a bit tougher than it could potentially be," said Carpenter.

"But after speaking to the coaches, understanding the game model going forward and hearing the signings that are coming in, I think it would have been very silly to leave."

title: How Arteta's response to Brighton loss may shape Arsenal's next chapter
description: Mikel Arteta has shown an increased appetite for risk this season but, as Arsenal look to stay at the top, failing to reinvent would be a greater gamble.
fullText:
Mikel Arteta has fashioned many versions of Arsenal.

Taking over a side in need of new life in 2019, he won the FA Cup in his first season by playing a defensive style of football, unafraid of using a back five.

As time passed the Gunners played a free-flowing style of attacking football - best seen in 2022 - before creating a side that reduced the variance of a match, maximised control and became physically difficult to compete with.

Having finally won the Premier League title, Arteta is reinventing his side again.

Perhaps freed by having lifted the trophy, we have seen the Spaniard take more gambles in personnel and tactics.

But, while an increased appetite for risk means the wins can be greater - so can the losses.

"Brighton were really good," Mikel Arteta confessed after Arsenal's 3-0 defeat before the international break.

Fabian Hurzeler masterminded the dominant victory against the reigning champions - defiantly opting against a pragmatic approach.

It is rare Arsenal are totally outclassed, so the loss to Brighton left a lingering sense of uncertainty going into the extended break.

But, given the timing of the defeat, it has been easy to forget that Arteta's men had won every game prior to that this season.

Last season, the heart of Arsenal had Martin Zubimendi at its base with Declan Rice in a more box-to-box role to the left of him.

Arsenal lost some momentum as the end of the season approached but it was the surprise use of Myles Lewis-Skelly in holding midfield that reinvigorated Arsenal, helping them over the line.

Arteta has since continued to trust the 20-year-old in that key role.

This season, Arsenal have used a 3-1-6 shape in possession, formed by Declan Rice dropping deep - rather than pushing on as he did in the first part of last season - to create a back three alongside Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes.

Lewis-Skelly plays as the single pivot, linking the back part and the front part of the team.

To label the rest of the team a 'front six' is perhaps an oversimplification, given the more specific roles certain players have.

Riccardo Calafiori, Ben White and Martin Odegaard take turns to drop deep, becoming a fifth player to Arsenal's base in moments. These dynamic arrivals, that create a '3-2' or a '4-1' base, require an alertness and reaction from the opposition to track them that isn't always possible.

These movements to drop deep therefore help Arsenal outnumber opponents, play around them and get up the pitch.

In William Saliba's absence, Konsa is a capable ball-playing centre-back. Rice, however, possesses both the passing and carrying quality of a world-class midfielder.

Facing forward and with more time and space on the ball, using him here maximises many of his strengths and minimises the amount of time he spends in small spaces with back to goal - a relative weakness for a player of his frame.

Lewis-Skelly has made that link position his own for reasons including his calmness under pressure, his hold-up strength, his ability to dribble past players one-v-one and his willingness to take risk - when deciding to dribble past a player or play direct passes for his attackers.

His effectiveness here has been noticed too by England boss Thomas Tuchel who, during this international break, has emulated Arteta's use of Lewis-Skelly.

For England it has been Elliot Anderson taking up the 'Declan Rice role' in the back three.

Given the demands of this role, part of the reason Arsenal may have struggled against Brighton was that Bruno Guimaraes took up this holding midfield position instead of Lewis-Skelly.

Hurzeler has drilled his Brighton side to play with high intensity, both on and off the ball. To play around their press requires superb technique, good positioning, the right timing of movements and an understanding of where team-mates may be.

These are things Guimaraes will get to grips with, given the time Lewis-Skelly has already had in this role, but being used in there against an effective Brighton man-to-man press was always going to be a difficult challenge.

Brighton's pressure meant Arsenal hesitated on the ball, forcing them to make decisions they normally wouldn't.

"You could see from the first throw-in, it was so clear. We put ourselves in trouble one, two, three times," Arteta said.

"We need to get out much quicker than that, and that's one of the biggest lessons we have to take from the game today."

After playing looser passes, Arsenal, known for their duelling, were beaten by a Brighton side that swarmed around the ball.

When Brighton were pushed deeper, Arsenal might've expected that things would play out like most games do for them - with them dominating the ball in the opposition's third against a low block.

From their settled defensive shape they picked moments to spring into a man-to-man press again - an effective solution that put Arteta's side under pressure throughout the match, preventing them from having an unmarked player to find.

Brighton prevailed because they created a game that was unfamiliar and unpredictable. Arsenal couldn't create the conditions they like to play out of.

If you are going to challenge Arsenal, this is the way to do so.

But, having seen how Brighton troubled his side, Arteta will be working to find solutions and make an unfamiliar challenge a more familiar one - as he did against Manchester City last season.

In last season's Carabao Cup final, Arsenal were caught out by a defensive tweak that led to City triumphing. Pep Guardiola opted for a zonal 4-2-4 shape that let Arsenal's defenders keep the ball but blocked access through the middle of the pitch.

City's new boss Enzo Maresca, knowing how effective this was, redeployed it against Arsenal in the Community Shield this season.

Arsenal had numerous solutions against this set-up, having had time to prepare, using their technical and versatile players in build-up.

As difficult as it is to overcome a man-to-man press executed as well as Brighton's, Arteta's track record suggests he will likely find ways to minimise its effectiveness against his side.

Arteta's response to Brighton, starting when they host Leeds on Saturday (12:30 BST), will be another chapter in his team's evolution - one that is both proactive and reactive.

This season we have seen Arteta encourage more asymmetrical and fluid play too, particularly down their right - a phenomenon worth its own deep-dive.

Kai Havertz has consistently moved over to the right touchline. White has arrived high up the pitch from a right-back position. Bukayo Saka has found himself on the wing or attacking centrally. Rice and Odegaard have come across to show for the ball too.

This new style of play, built on small-space combinations, fluidity and numerical overloads, has given Arsenal new answers to the same old low-block problem.

What all of this suggests is that Arteta is willing to move away from what has worked so well in previous seasons in the pursuit of new solutions, hoping to outrun a league looking to narrow the gap.

Such reinvention comes with teething problems, as Arsenal's struggles against Brighton showed.

But for a side looking to stay at the top, not reinventing may be a greater risk.

title: 'Different planet' Wilson becomes five-time MVP, but won't celebrate
description: A ceremony marking her record-extending fifth MVP award will take place on Friday night, but A'ja Wilson will not take part before a must-win game.
fullText:
While a ceremony marking her latest historic achievement will take place on Friday night, A'ja Wilson wants no part of it.

The 30-year-old Las Vegas Aces star stands peerless after becoming the first five-time Most Valuable Player (MVP) in WNBA history, and was informed of her unprecedented third-straight award by a former US vice-president.

But recent history means Wilson has no interest in joining the celebrations which will be held on her behalf.

When the Aces held a pre-game ceremony to honour Wilson last year, as is tradition for the MVP winner, they went on to lose game one of their play-off semi-final.

They also lost heavily following similar celebrations after receiving their championship rings in May.

Before a must-win third game in their best-of-five semi-final against the Golden State Valkyries, Wilson is taking no chances.

"I love the fans, but I will not be doing that," she said. "I will be warming up with my team. Everyone knows how much of a competitor I am [and] what my main focus is."

No other WNBA player has won more than three MVP awards.

Having also won in 2020 and 2022, Wilson joins NBA legends Michael Jordan and Bill Russell as five-time MVP winners. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar won six.

"I've said [before] 'Take her off Mount Rushmore, she's Everest," Aces coach Becky Hammon said.

"Now, I'm taking her off Everest and I just have to put her on a different planet."

Wilson, who received 65 of 74 first-place votes, received a voice message from former vice-president Kamala Harris delivering the news.

Despite her extensive list of honours, Wilson was very emotional after receiving her latest MVP award on the Aces' practice court.

"When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out and you just never imagine you will be able to check them off," Wilson said

"I think that's why I cried a little bit harder on this one because 15-year-old A'ja wasn't sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP, she wasn't dreaming about being a three-time champion, she was dreaming about surviving this world."

Wilson averaged 26.2 points to lead the league in scoring for the third straight season.

An eight-time All-Star, she registered at least 20 points in 33 games - the third-highest single-season streak in WNBA history, and tied her own WNBA single-season record of scoring at least 30 points in 13 games.

Wilson has won three league titles with the Aces - achieved in the past four years - but they face elimination in this year's semi-finals as they trail Golden State 2-0.

title: Wimbledon boss jokes military would love to 'sort out' influencers
description: Royal Marine Commandos providing security at Wimbledon would like "nothing more than to sort out" disruptive social media influencers at the prestigious tournament, its chief executive jokes.
fullText:
Royal Marine commandos providing security at Wimbledon would like "nothing more than to sort out" disruptive social media influencers at the prestigious tournament, its chief executive has joked.

US Open organisers accredited 100 influencers and content creators for this year's tournament.

But when a match involving two-time champion Naomi Osaka was disrupted by a group of influencers conducting a photo shoot, it prompted a debate about tennis etiquette.

Richard Atkinson, interim chief executive at the All England Lawn Tennis Club, said Wimbledon did not offer accreditation to influencers and sources have indicated to BBC Sport that is unlikely to change in the near future.

While Atkinson acknowledged that influencers were a "crucial part of the marketing mix" and to ban them from attending the tournament entirely would be "nonsense", he said any that were brought in by brands would be "tightly chaperoned".

He also backed the traditional "self-policing" ethos at SW19, whereby fans respect the action.

After the disruption at the US Open, world number four Coco Gauff said it was important to welcome a "new demographic" to the sport, but said: "I think it's just, follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."

And Wimbledon's boss made it clear he does not expect to see a repeat at the All England Club.

"We don't have a category of accredited people called influencers," Atkinson told a panel at Leaders Week London.

"That said, clearly influencers are a crucial part of building your brand around the world in the third decade of the 21st century.

"What you have to do is keep them under control. One of our big partners, Polo Ralph Lauren, will have their influencer, but they are all tightly chaperoned."

He said the atmosphere at the US Open is "very New York City", adding: "It's dead easy for someone who has just bought a ticket to show up there with their ring lights and literally start broadcasting in the middle of a match.

"If you tried to do that at Wimbledon, I think you'd probably have some Royal Marine Commando…"

He then joked: "We do have military. And they would like nothing more, I suspect, than to sort out some influencer."

Fans will also not be allowed to bring portable ring lights - a piece of equipment used by content creators - to SW19.

Atkinson did, however, point out that the media landscape has changed, and suggested there is a place for embracing influencers and content creators to ensure Wimbledon remains relevant.

"It's just a crucial bit of the marketing mix, of course it is," he said.

"We're not in the world of newspapers and television anymore, right? The world has changed. But it's just really important, it's a bit of a cliched expression, you've got to sort it out in a Wimbledon way. But to say "we're not going to have any influencers at Wimbledon", it's obviously nonsense."

"Our marketing team work meticulously to make sure they are working in a way that is consistent with our Wimbledon brand and keeps that magic that I was referring to earlier."

title: Mourinho calls criticism of Mbappe 'ridiculous'
description: Jose Mourinho defends Kylian Mbappe who has been scrutinised during the international break.
fullText:
Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho has defended Kylian Mbappe over his activities during the international break - describing criticism as "ridiculous".

France captain Mbappe withdrew from international duty after picking up an injury against Turkey on 25 September.

He later shared images on social media at a Paris Fashion Week event and also riding a bicycle - something Mourinho had previously said was against his rules.

"When it comes to Real Madrid, it's always different," he said.

"But all the players did exactly what they were supposed to during the break. And then you always want to look for more problems and issues.

"What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to and when he fails at that and he stops being a Real Madrid player for 24 hours, you will not see that player on the bench because he will be at home."

He said an image of Mbappe riding a bike in Switzerland had been misrepresented, saying that bicycles were available for guests at his hotel complex to use for short journeys.

Asked if coverage of Mbappe was exaggerated he added: "Exaggerated, no - I think it was ridiculous.

"If Mbappe plays tomorrow, it's because he hasn't failed Real Madrid and he hasn't failed to fulfil his obligations to the club," he added.

Real are six points behind leaders Barcelona in the La Liga table after seven games.

Mbappe, 27, is one of the favourites to win this year's Ballon d'Or. He scored 42 goals in 44 games for his club last season but they did not win any trophies.

He won the World Cup Golden Boot with 10 goals, taking his career tally at World Cups to a record 22 - although France finished fourth.

title: Legendary Leeds Rhinos winger Hall retires
description: Leeds Rhinos legend Ryan Hall announces his retirement at the age of 38.
fullText:
Leeds Rhinos legend Ryan Hall has announced his retirement at the age of 38.

The winger made his senior debut for the Rhinos in May 2007 and went on to score 358 tries in 540 career appearances.

The former England international, who also had spells with Sydney Roosters and Hull KR, won six Grand Finals and two Challenge Cups with Leeds.

"I think the time's right that I hang up the boots. I've done it for 20 years and I've loved every minute of it," he told the club website., external

"The club's in a good position to go with the youth, that's the natural progression in rugby league."

Hall, who will move into a commercial role at the club, is Super League's second highest scorer with 274, seven behind Leigh winger Josh Charnley.

He left Leeds for Sydney Roosters after the 2018 season but failed to score a try in 11 NRL appearances across two seasons.

Hull KR brought him back to Super League for the 2021 campaign and he scored 62 tries in 102 games for the Robins before returning to Leeds two years ago.

He scored 10 times in 24 appearances in 2026 as the Rhinos finished second and his final appearance for the club came in their play-off semi-final defeat by Warrington at Headingley.

"I am pleased to have had the honour to work with Ryan over the last couple of years," head coach Brad Arthur said.

"He has performed at the very highest level for his club and country and he leaves the field on his terms, having maintained his presence for 20 years; that is a remarkable achievement."

The club have said Hall, who scored 39 tries in 40 appearances for England and was part of the side that finished runner-up in the 2017 World Cup final, will make a "cameo appearance" in a pre-season match against Hull FC in January as part of a testimonial.

title: James suffers defeat on 76ers debut in pre-season
description: LeBron James says it's "going to take some time" for his new team-mates to gel after suffering defeat on his debut for the Philadelphia 76ers in a pre-season game.
fullText:
LeBron James said it's "going to take some time" for his new team-mates to gel after suffering defeat on his debut for the Philadelphia 76ers in a pre-season game.

The 41-year-old American joined the 76ers in July for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA following a glittering career.

James is the highest points scorer in the history of the league and is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season.

James scored 10 points and added four rebounds, five assists and a steal in 18 first-half minutes as his side fell to a 114-108 defeat by the Brooklyn Nets.

"We're still trying to put each other in the position to be successful and complement each other the best way we can on the floor. But it's going to take some time," said James.

"Tonight was a good sample size for us to build on."

James played alongside new team-mates Joel Embiid, VJ Edgecombe, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, with the latter leading the scoring with 18 points.

James has won titles with every NBA side he has played for, including two with the Miami Heat, one with the Cleveland Cavaliers and another with the Los Angeles Lakers.

He left the Lakers this summer after spending eight years with the franchise.

James has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and has been an NBA All-Star the last 22 seasons running.

He is aiming to help the 76ers win their first NBA title in 43 years.

title: Is £70m Baleba ready for his Man Utd exam?
description: Manchester United's £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is expected to make his debut against Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford
fullText:
Carlos Baleba has come a long way since the day he had to pull out of a Cameroon Cup last-16 match due to a school exam.

Now Baleba's exams tend to be restricted to the football field - and a significant one is looming at Old Trafford this weekend.

It is unfair on the 22-year-old to be viewed as the potential saviour of Manchester United's season.

However, at £70m, Baleba was by far the most expensive of United's three major summer signings.

He is also the player earmarked for the holding midfield role Michael Carrick has had trouble filling effectively following Casemiro's exit in May.

United knew Baleba had an ankle injury when they bought him from Brighton on 25 August and they may have to wait until after the international break for the Cameroon midfielder to make his debut.

They were not expecting that they would be 12th in the Premier League, with just one win and five points from their opening five games. In addition, Brighton came from 2-0 down at Old Trafford to deservedly knock them out of the EFL Cup.

So there is no disguising that the pressure is on for Baleba and his new club ahead of the visit of rock-bottom Tottenham before three away trips in a row. Champions League encounters at Atletico Madrid and Como fall either side of a journey across the Pennines to face Leeds.

"Very quick," is the assessment from one United insider of their first impressions of Baleba. "He covers the ground really well."

A handful of training sessions before Baleba was named on the bench for the 1-1 draw at Fulham on 20 September, and a closed doors game against Swiss League outfit Lausanne-Sports on 2 October, when United's international contingent were absent, is a small sample size to form an opinion on.

However, Baleba's speed is something that should bring positive benefits to United's midfield.

Andrey Santos has it; less so Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans, who have been paired together by Carrick in the last four league games due to their superior technical abilities.

United have been too easy to play through and danger has not been spotted quickly enough.

Carrick's side is one of only four in the top flight yet to keep a clean sheet. They have conceded twice in four out of their seven games in all competitions. Until an answer is found, an upturn in form is difficult to envisage.

Clearly, Baleba must do a bit more than run fast, and his input must be felt in the dressing room as well as on the pitch.

Sources say an understandable initial shyness and nervousness seems to be being overcome. Baleba is not the most confident English speaker, but he has improved significantly since he moved to Brighton from Lille for £23.2m in 2023.

He has struck up a friendship with Amad Diallo. It is coincidence two young players from Africa should be going through their recovery work at the same time, but also helpful that a shared background creates a natural bond that has been built on over the last few weeks.

Amad was even laughing on the video he uploaded onto social media of Baleba poking fun at him after Cameroon beat his Ivory Coast in a friendly on 3 October.

A former team-mate of new France international Leny Yoro at Lille and Bryan Mbeumo at international level, Baleba already has other unexpected relationships at United's Carrington training ground judging by his joking with Patrick Dorgu after the final game of last season at the Amex Stadium.

The key for United is that Baleba produces the performances that lit up his 2024-25 campaign and earned suggestions of a potential move to Real Madrid, rather than those last term which were often below-par.

Suggestions Baleba had his head turned by late interest from United in the summer of 2025 have been dismissed by Brighton sources, although an alternative reason for the dip in form has not been offered.

As it turned out, the background work done by the data and recruitment teams at Carrington 12 months ago was not wasted. After missing out on Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, and with other options deemed unsuitable, United moved for Baleba just before the shock opening-day defeat at Hull, completing the deal just afterwards.

Given they were being quoted significantly more than £100m for the midfielder in August 2025, they regard £70m as good business.

However, Baleba is yet to step on the pitch and as Fernandes has shown in his disappointing early performances for Tottenham, any early assessment of what constitutes a good deal should at least wait for that.

It will be fascinating to see how Baleba and Fernandes match up to each other if they start at Old Trafford, when defeat for either side has the potential to turn early season disappointment into a near crisis.

Baleba's natural jocular personality should help his preparation. He will hope to get the chance to show off his back flip goal celebration – even if an ability to find the net is not why United bought him.

More importantly though, he has a powerful determination to succeed, drilled into him by his dad. He pushed him through punishing training sessions when he was younger, which Baleba has said was integral to him becoming a professional.

In a sense, success has already been achieved given he has fulfilled a promise he made to his mum to build her a house in Douala. Tragically for Baleba, his mother died a few months before he left Lille and never saw it.

He is still pushing, still motivated to do well for her, as he recounted in an interview with the Guardian in April 2025.

Go back further, to a chat with French football magazine Onze Mondial in September 2023 and you get to the core of what makes Baleba tick.

In explaining his passions outside of football, Baleba talks about manga, described by the British Museum as 'Japanese comic books or graphic novels', which now has 'fans across the globe'.

His favourite series is Fist of the North Star, the hero of which is Kenshiro.

"When he started out, everyone beat him up, he got covered in scars, then he became strong," Baleba explained. "After that, he was the one beating everyone up. He never gave up. I like that attitude."
